domain_name: Information Systems Acquisition, Development and Implementation

questions.question: An IS auditor wants evidence that a new project's manager was formally given authority over project resources. Which document is MOST appropriate to examine?

options.A: The work breakdown structure and its task schedule
options.B: The project risk register with assigned response owners
options.C: The project charter approved by the sponsor
options.D: The approved business case and feasibility study

questions.key_concept: The project charter formally authorizes a project, names its sponsor and grants the project manager authority over resources.
questions.pre_read: Separate documents that justify a project from the one that authorizes it and delegates authority.
questions.correct_explanation: The project charter is the document that formally authorizes the project, names the sponsor and grants the project manager authority to use organizational resources. The business case is the runner-up: it justifies the investment and supports the decision to proceed, but it does not delegate authority to a named project manager.

wrong_explanations.A: The work breakdown structure is a planning artifact produced after authorization. It decomposes deliverables but grants no one authority.
wrong_explanations.B: The risk register records threats and responses during planning and execution. It does not authorize the project or its manager.
wrong_explanations.D: The business case justifies the investment and feeds the go decision, but authority over resources is delegated in the charter.

tips: Eliminate: A and B are planning artifacts created after the project is authorized, so neither can grant authority.
Final two: C beats D because the business case justifies funding, while the charter actually delegates authority to the project manager.
Exam cue: when the stem asks who authorized a project or its manager, look for the sponsor-approved charter.
questions.framework_ref: PMBOK Guide 6th Edition, Section 4.1 (Develop Project Charter); PRINCE2 (Projects in Controlled Environments); ISACA Project Management Audit/Assurance Program

questions.question: An IS auditor finds that developers began coding a new application before user requirements were signed off. What is the GREATEST risk?

options.A: Unit tests will cover fewer code paths than planned
options.B: Release scheduling will need a longer change freeze
options.C: Later rework will push project costs over budget
options.D: The delivered system may not meet business needs

questions.key_concept: Approved requirements are the baseline every later SDLC phase builds on; skipping them risks a system that misses business needs.
questions.pre_read: Recall the SDLC order and ask what each phase hands to the next. Then weigh outcome risk against symptom risk.
questions.correct_explanation: In a linear SDLC each phase produces artifacts that feed the next, and approved requirements are the baseline for design, build and testing. Coding without them means the system may be built to the wrong target and fail to deliver business value. Cost overrun from rework is the runner-up: it is real, but it is a symptom of the larger risk of not meeting business needs.

wrong_explanations.A: Test coverage depends on the test strategy, not on requirements sign-off timing. It is a minor technical concern here.
wrong_explanations.B: Change-freeze length relates to deployment planning. It has no direct link to skipping the requirements phase.
wrong_explanations.C: Rework and overruns are likely, but they follow from the core problem: building something the business did not agree to.

tips: Eliminate: A is a testing-coverage detail and B is a deployment-scheduling issue; neither follows from skipping requirements approval.
Final two: D beats C because failing to meet business needs is the root risk; cost overrun is one consequence of it.
Exam cue: when a phase is skipped, pick the option about the business outcome over its cost or schedule symptoms.

questions.question: Before go-live, an IS auditor must confirm that a new payroll system passes data correctly to the general ledger and bank interfaces. Which testing evidence is MOST appropriate?

options.A: Integration test results tracing records across each connection
options.B: Acceptance test results signed off by the payroll business owners
options.C: Unit test results logged by the individual developers
options.D: Code coverage reports produced by the build pipeline

questions.key_concept: Each test level has its own scope: unit for modules, integration for interfaces between components, system for the whole, UAT for business acceptance.
questions.pre_read: Match the audit objective in the stem to the test level whose scope covers it.
questions.correct_explanation: Integration testing is the level designed to verify that data passes correctly between connected components and systems, so its results directly evidence the payroll-to-ledger and bank flows. Business acceptance sign-off is the runner-up: it shows users accept the workflows, but users judge business outcomes on selected scenarios and do not systematically verify every interface record.

wrong_explanations.B: Acceptance confirms the system meets user needs. It is not designed to verify each interface's data transfer systematically.
wrong_explanations.C: Unit tests verify single modules in isolation. They cannot show that data moves correctly between systems.
wrong_explanations.D: Coverage reports measure how much code the tests exercised. They say nothing about interface data accuracy.

tips: Eliminate: C tests modules in isolation and D measures code exercised; neither examines data passing between systems.
Final two: A beats B because integration testing is designed to verify interface data flows, while UAT confirms business acceptance.
Exam cue: match the objective to the test level: interfaces point to integration testing, business fit to UAT.

questions.question: An IS auditor finds that a release's source code is baselined, but its approved design specifications can be edited freely. Which conclusion is MOST appropriate?

options.A: Design documents are no longer needed once the code is baselined
options.B: The baseline is incomplete; specifications should be configuration items
options.C: Specification edits should be raised as entries in the defect tracker
options.D: Specification changes should be noted at the next release review

questions.key_concept: Configuration items include code, designs, requirements and builds; all must be under formal change control as part of the baseline.
questions.pre_read: Ask what belongs in a product baseline. Then compare control before a change with review after it.
questions.correct_explanation: A configuration item is any identified artifact placed under formal change control as part of the product baseline, including requirements, designs, code and build files. Uncontrolled specifications mean the baseline cannot be trusted. Noting changes at the next release review is the runner-up: it adds visibility, but only after the fact, so unauthorized edits can still reach the baseline.

wrong_explanations.A: Design specifications remain essential for maintenance, testing and impact analysis. Code alone does not form a complete product baseline.
wrong_explanations.C: A defect tracker records faults found in testing. It is not a change-control mechanism for approved documents.
wrong_explanations.D: Reviewing edits later is detective and delayed. Configuration management requires formal control before a baselined item changes.

tips: Eliminate: A discards artifacts the baseline needs, and C confuses defect tracking with configuration change control.
Final two: B beats D because formal change control over every baselined artifact prevents unauthorized edits; a later review only notices them.
Exam cue: a configuration item is any controlled artifact in the baseline, not just code, and not just hardware.
questions.framework_ref: IEEE 828 (Configuration Management in Systems and Software Engineering); ISO/IEC 12207 (Software Life Cycle Processes); ITIL 4 Service Configuration Management; COBIT 2019 BAI10 (Managed Configuration)

questions.question: An IS auditor reviews a project's risk register. Which condition BEST justifies the project manager escalating a risk to the sponsor?

options.A: The risk was re-rated higher in the most recent risk assessment
options.B: The risk owner set a response date two periods out
options.C: The mitigating vendor has not yet signed a contract
options.D: Residual exposure exceeds the manager's delegated tolerance

questions.key_concept: Project risks are escalated when residual exposure exceeds delegated tolerance or the response needs authority beyond the manager's mandate.
questions.pre_read: Think about delegated authority. Ask which option shows the project manager can no longer decide alone.
questions.correct_explanation: Escalation is driven by authority: when residual exposure exceeds the tolerance the project manager was delegated, or a response needs authority beyond that mandate, the decision belongs to the sponsor. A higher re-rating is the runner-up: it signals a worsening risk, but the manager may still be able to treat it within existing tolerance.

wrong_explanations.A: A higher rating is a useful signal, but if exposure stays within the manager's tolerance it can be handled without escalating.
wrong_explanations.B: A scheduled response date shows the risk is being managed. It is not a trigger for sponsor involvement.
wrong_explanations.C: An unsigned vendor contract is an operational issue to resolve within the project. It does not by itself exceed delegated authority.

tips: Eliminate: B shows normal risk management in progress, and C is an operational task the project can resolve itself.
Final two: D beats A because escalation follows delegated tolerance and authority; a re-rating alone may still sit within the manager's limits.
Exam cue: escalate when a risk exceeds the tolerance or authority delegated to the current level, not merely when it changes.

questions.question: A steering committee is choosing between options for a seven-year platform investment whose largest benefits arrive after year three. Which metric should be its PRIMARY basis?

options.A: Payback period, showing how quickly the cost is recovered
options.B: Hardware purchase cost within the first budget year
options.C: Net present value of the discounted cash flows
options.D: Number of user stories delivered in each release

questions.key_concept: NPV suits long-horizon investments with material later cash flows; payback suits decisions dominated by liquidity and quick recovery.
questions.pre_read: Notice the time horizon and when the benefits arrive. Ask which metric counts cash flows after cost is recovered.
questions.correct_explanation: Net present value discounts every expected cash flow over the whole investment life, so it reflects the time value of money and the large benefits arriving after year three. Payback period is the runner-up: it is useful when liquidity or quick recovery dominates, but it ignores cash flows after the payback point, which here carry most of the value.

wrong_explanations.A: Payback ignores both the time value of money and benefits after recovery. With value concentrated late, it would understate the strongest option.
wrong_explanations.B: First-year hardware cost covers a fraction of total cost and none of the benefits. It cannot rank long-term investments.
wrong_explanations.D: Story counts measure delivery throughput, not financial value. They have no place as an investment-selection metric.

tips: Eliminate: B looks only at a slice of first-year cost, and D is a delivery metric with no financial value.
Final two: C beats A because NPV captures late benefits and the time value of money; payback stops counting once cost is recovered.
Exam cue: long horizon and late benefits point to NPV; tight cash and fast recovery point to payback.

questions.question: An IS auditor must confirm that every approved requirement for a new system was built and tested. Which evidence is MOST useful?

options.A: A traceability matrix linking requirements to test results
options.B: Business sign-off on the final acceptance test cycle
options.C: Code review records showing coding standards were met
options.D: The release log of deployments made to production

questions.key_concept: A requirements traceability matrix links each requirement to design, code and tests, proving completeness and supporting change impact analysis.
questions.pre_read: Look for the word every in the stem. Ask which evidence maps each requirement individually rather than approving the whole.
questions.correct_explanation: A requirements traceability matrix links each approved requirement forward to its design, code and test cases, so the auditor can spot any requirement with no test or no result. Acceptance sign-off is the runner-up: it shows users accepted what they tested, but it cannot show that every requirement was covered by a test.

wrong_explanations.B: Sign-off confirms acceptance of the tests that were run. Without traceability, untested requirements would go unnoticed.
wrong_explanations.C: Code reviews check how code was written. They do not map code back to approved requirements.
wrong_explanations.D: A deployment log records what was released and when. It does not show which requirements were built or tested.

tips: Eliminate: C checks coding style, and D records deployments; neither maps requirements to tests.
Final two: A beats B because completeness needs a requirement-by-requirement link; sign-off covers only what was actually tested.
Exam cue: 'every requirement built and tested' is a completeness question; look for traceability, not approval.

questions.question: A project manager wants reliable release forecasts from a newly formed Scrum team's velocity. Which practice is MOST appropriate?

options.A: Convert story points into hours to fix each sprint's commitments
options.B: Use team-relative sizing and forecast once velocity stabilizes
options.C: Have the product owner assign story points alone
options.D: Reset velocity to zero at the start of each release

questions.key_concept: Agile velocity forecasts become reliable when the team sizes work relatively and velocity has stabilized over several sprints.
questions.pre_read: Remember that velocity is empirical. Ask which option builds a trustworthy history rather than imposing precision.
questions.correct_explanation: Velocity is an empirical measure: it becomes a reliable forecasting input only when the same team sizes work relative to its own past stories and several sprints of data have accumulated. Converting points to hours is the runner-up because it sounds precise, but it abandons relative sizing and turns estimates into time commitments the team cannot yet support.

wrong_explanations.A: Hours conversion defeats relative sizing and creates false precision. It does not make a new team's forecasts more reliable.
wrong_explanations.C: Sizing by one person loses the team's shared judgement. Points stop reflecting the effort of those doing the work.
wrong_explanations.D: Resetting velocity throws away the history that makes forecasting possible. It increases, not reduces, uncertainty.

tips: Eliminate: C removes team ownership of estimates, and D discards the very history forecasting depends on.
Final two: B beats A because agile forecasting relies on stabilized empirical velocity; converting to hours adds false precision.
Exam cue: in agile, reliability comes from team-owned estimates and observed history, not from fixed-hour commitments.

questions.question: An IS auditor reviews a CI/CD pipeline that deploys to production several times a day. Which control provides the GREATEST assurance over build quality?

options.A: Developer attestation that known defects have been resolved
options.B: Quarterly penetration testing of the current production release
options.C: Automated nightly regression test runs against the main code branch
options.D: Automated gates that block deployment on failed tests or scans

questions.key_concept: In CI/CD, automated quality gates that block deployment on failed tests or scans give consistent preventive assurance for every build.
questions.pre_read: Note the deployment frequency. Ask which control acts on every build before production rather than afterwards.
questions.correct_explanation: With several deployments a day, only an enforced control in the pipeline can act on every build before it reaches production. Gates that fail the build on test or scan failures are preventive and consistent. Nightly automated regression runs are the runner-up: they are consistent, but they are detective and run after many builds have already been deployed.

wrong_explanations.A: Self-attestation is unverified and not independent. It gives little assurance that defects were really fixed.
wrong_explanations.B: Quarterly testing examines a tiny fraction of releases. Hundreds of builds would reach production untested in between.
wrong_explanations.C: Nightly runs are automated but detective. They test code after it has already been deployed several times that day.

tips: Eliminate: A relies on unverified self-attestation, and B tests far too rarely for daily deployments.
Final two: D beats C because an enforced gate stops every bad build before release; a nightly run only finds problems afterward.
Exam cue: in high-frequency pipelines, prefer preventive gates in the deployment flow over checks that run after release, automated or not.

questions.question: Developers request production customer data to populate a new test environment. Which control should the IS auditor MOST expect to see?

options.A: Encryption of the test database with identifiers left intact
options.B: Signed confidentiality agreements from each requesting developer
options.C: Masking of personal data before it is extracted
options.D: Nightly restores of last month's production backup

questions.key_concept: Production-derived test data should be masked or pseudonymized before extraction, so non-production environments never hold real personal data.
questions.pre_read: Ask who can see the data once it is in test. Prefer controls that remove exposure over controls that guard it.
questions.correct_explanation: Masking or pseudonymizing personal data before extraction means the test environment never holds recoverable personal data, which applies data protection by design. Encryption at rest is the runner-up: it protects stored data from theft of the media, but anyone using the test system still sees real identifiers.

wrong_explanations.A: Encryption at rest protects against stolen media, but authorized test users still see real personal data in clear text.
wrong_explanations.B: Agreements deter misuse but do not reduce exposure. Real personal data still sits in a less controlled environment.
wrong_explanations.D: Restoring production backups copies all personal data into test unchanged, maximizing exposure.

tips: Eliminate: B relies on a signature, not a control on the data, and D copies production data wholesale.
Final two: C beats A because masking removes personal data from test entirely; encryption still exposes it to every test user.
Exam cue: for test data, remove the sensitive content at the source rather than protecting it after it has been copied.

questions.question: A development manager asks an IS auditor where static application security testing adds the MOST value. Which recommendation is BEST?

options.A: Scan each pull request and fail builds on high-severity findings
options.B: Scan each release candidate before the change board reviews it
options.C: Scan the production code base quarterly to track long-term trends
options.D: Route findings to the security team to forward critical items

questions.key_concept: SAST adds most value when run on every pull request, with builds failing on high-severity findings: shift left, fast feedback.
questions.pre_read: Think about when a flaw is cheapest to fix. Compare an early enforced check with a later one.
questions.correct_explanation: Static testing is most effective early and often: scanning each pull request gives developers fast feedback while the code is fresh, and failing builds on high-severity findings stops flaws from progressing. Scanning release candidates is the runner-up: it still finds flaws before production, but late in the cycle, when fixes are slower and costlier and may delay the release.

wrong_explanations.B: Release-candidate scans catch flaws late. Fixes then compete with release dates, and pressure to accept risk rises.
wrong_explanations.C: Quarterly scans of production find flaws only after they are live. They measure trends rather than prevent defects.
wrong_explanations.D: Filtering findings through another team slows feedback and leaves most issues unfixed. Developers lose ownership of secure code.

tips: Eliminate: C scans production code long after release, and D delays and filters feedback away from developers.
Final two: A beats B because shifting scans left to each pull request fixes flaws earliest and cheapest; release-time scans come late.
Exam cue: for security testing in development, choose the earliest enforced point that gives developers fast feedback.

questions.question: An IS auditor must confirm that customer balances migrated completely and accurately to a new core platform. Which evidence is BEST?

options.A: User acceptance test results for the main business workflows
options.B: Record counts and control totals reconciled source to target
options.C: Load test results at projected transaction volumes
options.D: Regression results showing the legacy system still runs

questions.key_concept: Data conversion integrity is evidenced by source-to-target reconciliation of record counts and control totals, with variances investigated.
questions.pre_read: Focus on the words completely and accurately. Ask which evidence compares the data itself, not the system's behavior.
questions.correct_explanation: Completeness and accuracy of converted data are proven by reconciling the source and target: matching record counts, control totals and hash totals, with every variance investigated. User acceptance results are the runner-up: they show the new system's workflows work for users, but they test functions on sample data rather than proving every balance arrived intact.

wrong_explanations.A: Acceptance testing checks that workflows function. It does not prove that every migrated record and amount matches the source.
wrong_explanations.C: Load testing shows the platform handles volume. It says nothing about whether the migrated data is correct.
wrong_explanations.D: Legacy regression results concern the old system's operation, not the integrity of data moved to the new one.

tips: Eliminate: C tests capacity, and D tests the old system; neither addresses migrated data.
Final two: B beats A because reconciliation proves every record and total transferred; acceptance testing only shows functions work.
Exam cue: for data conversion, completeness and accuracy evidence means counts and control totals matched between source and target.

questions.question: An IS auditor reviews the terms of reference for a change advisory board. Which responsibility should be the board's PRIMARY role?

options.A: Writing the technical implementation plan for each change
options.B: Running high-risk deployments in production personally
options.C: Assessing risk and readiness of significant changes
options.D: Reviewing completed changes afterwards to capture lessons learned

questions.key_concept: A change advisory board assesses the risk, impact and readiness of significant changes before authorization; it neither plans nor executes them.
questions.pre_read: Separate governance from execution. Then ask whether the board's main value comes before or after a change.
questions.correct_explanation: The change advisory board is a governance body: it assesses the risk, impact and readiness of significant changes so they can be authorized before deployment. Post-implementation review is the runner-up: boards may take part in it, but looking back at completed changes supports improvement rather than the board's primary job of authorizing change before it happens.

wrong_explanations.A: Implementation plans are written by the technical teams requesting the change. The board reviews them; it does not author them.
wrong_explanations.B: Deployment is executed by operations staff. Board members running changes would blur oversight and execution.
wrong_explanations.D: Reviews after implementation support learning, but the board's primary value is assessing changes before they are made.

tips: Eliminate: A and B are delivery tasks for technical staff; a governance board should not author or execute changes.
Final two: C beats D because the board's primary role is assessing changes before authorization; post-implementation review is secondary.
Exam cue: governance bodies review and authorize; they do not write plans or execute work themselves.

questions.question: A QA manager reports that defect density per KLOC doubled after a new test team joined. What should the IS auditor do FIRST?

options.A: Conclude that code quality has declined across the release
options.B: Report the project as over budget to the steering committee
options.C: Record the rise as evidence of higher developer productivity
options.D: Analyze root causes to separate better detection from worse code

questions.key_concept: Rising defect density can reflect better testing or worse code; root-cause analysis must come before any conclusion.
questions.pre_read: Notice what changed at the same time as the metric. Ask whether a conclusion is justified yet.
questions.correct_explanation: A rise in defect density can mean more thorough testing finds more defects, or that the code itself got worse. A new test team makes both plausible, so the auditor must analyze root causes before concluding. Declining code quality is the runner-up: it is a natural reading, but concluding it first ignores that better detection could explain the change.

wrong_explanations.A: Worse code is one possible cause, but the new test team could equally explain the rise. Concluding first is premature.
wrong_explanations.B: Defect density measures defects per thousand lines of code. It does not measure cost or budget variance.
wrong_explanations.C: More defects per line of code does not indicate productivity. The metric has no link to output rates.

tips: Eliminate: B treats a quality metric as a cost measure, and C treats it as a productivity measure.
Final two: D beats A because a change in detection could explain the rise; the auditor confirms the cause before concluding.
Exam cue: when a metric moves after a change in how it is measured, investigate the cause before drawing conclusions.

questions.question: An organization is buying business-critical custom software from a small start-up vendor. Which contract provision should the IS auditor MOST recommend?

options.A: Source code escrow with defined release conditions
options.B: A right-to-audit clause over the vendor's development process
options.C: Offsite backups of the organization's own internal code
options.D: Annual price caps on maintenance and support fees

questions.key_concept: Source code escrow protects continuity of business-critical custom software when the vendor may fail or stop supporting it.
questions.pre_read: Identify the main risk: the vendor might not survive. Ask which provision still works after the vendor is gone.
questions.correct_explanation: Escrow places the source code with an independent agent and releases it if defined events occur, such as vendor failure. For business-critical custom software from a vendor whose survival is uncertain, that protects continuity. A right-to-audit clause is the runner-up: it gives visibility into how the vendor builds software, but it does nothing if the vendor stops trading.

wrong_explanations.B: Audit rights help assess development quality while the vendor operates. They provide no access to source code if it fails.
wrong_explanations.C: Backing up internal code does not cover vendor-owned source code. The continuity gap remains.
wrong_explanations.D: Price caps control cost. They do not address the risk of losing support for critical software.

tips: Eliminate: C protects the wrong code, and D addresses cost rather than continuity of support.
Final two: A beats B because escrow secures source code if the vendor fails; audit rights only give visibility while it operates.
Exam cue: critical custom software plus a fragile single vendor points to escrow with clear release triggers.

questions.question: Six months after go-live, an IS auditor performs a post-implementation review of a CRM system. What is the PRIMARY focus of the review?

options.A: Project spending by phase against the approved budget
options.B: Realized benefits compared with the approved business case
options.C: A final round of acceptance tests on functional requirements
options.D: The regression test plan for the next maintenance window

questions.key_concept: A post-implementation review primarily compares realized benefits with the approved business case to confirm value delivery.
questions.pre_read: Remember why the project was approved. Ask which option tests whether that promise was kept.
questions.correct_explanation: A post-implementation review asks whether the investment delivered the value it promised: the realized benefits and outcomes are compared with those in the approved business case. Spending against budget is the runner-up: cost performance is reviewed at closure, but staying on budget does not show that the system is delivering its intended business value.

wrong_explanations.A: Budget variance matters at project closure, but a project can stay on budget and still fail to deliver the promised benefits.
wrong_explanations.C: Acceptance testing belongs before go-live. Six months into operation, the question is value delivered, not functional sign-off.
wrong_explanations.D: Regression planning is an ongoing maintenance activity. It is not the purpose of a post-implementation review.

tips: Eliminate: C repeats a pre-go-live activity, and D is routine maintenance planning, not a review of outcomes.
Final two: B beats A because the review's main question is value delivered against the business case; budget performance is secondary.
Exam cue: post-implementation reviews look back to the business case: did the promised benefits actually arrive?

questions.subtopic: SDLC Methodology Selection. Regulated vs Agile
questions.question: A health insurer's CIO wants Scrum-only delivery for a regulated claims platform that undergoes annual SOC 1 audits. Which approach should the IS auditor MOST recommend?

options.A: Pure Scrum, using sprint reviews as the audit evidence
options.B: Waterfall, with signed phase deliverables as audit evidence
options.C: Scrum, with a single compliance sign-off before final release
options.D: Hybrid agile with stage gates and signed traceability baselines

questions.key_concept: Regulated projects can use agile delivery when stage gates, signed baselines and traceability give auditors the evidence they need.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the regulator and auditor need to see. Then look for the option that provides it without discarding agility.
questions.correct_explanation: A hybrid keeps agile delivery while adding the controls regulators and auditors rely on: stage gates, signed requirements baselines, traceability and controlled scope changes. Strict waterfall is the runner-up: it produces strong evidence, but it assumes agile cannot be controlled and gives up delivery flexibility the organization values, when a hybrid can satisfy both needs.

wrong_explanations.A: Sprint reviews show working increments but leave no signed baselines or traceability. Auditors would lack evidence over requirements and changes.
wrong_explanations.B: Waterfall yields strong evidence but gives up the delivery flexibility the CIO wants, when agile with gates and baselines can satisfy regulators too.
wrong_explanations.C: One sign-off at the end gives no stage gates or traceability during delivery, so gaps surface when they are costliest to fix.

tips: Eliminate: A drops the traceability that regulated audits need, and C checks compliance once, at the end, when gaps are costliest to fix.
Final two: D beats B because a controlled hybrid meets evidence needs and keeps agility; waterfall needlessly sacrifices delivery flexibility.
Exam cue: in regulated agile projects, recommend adding gates and traceability to agile rather than abandoning agile.

questions.question: Four weeks before an ERP go-live, only 47% of UAT cases have passed against agreed exit criteria. What is the IS auditor's MOST appropriate recommendation to the steering committee?

options.A: Re-scope UAT to remove failing cases so the criteria are met
options.B: Have the audit team re-execute the failed cases independently
options.C: Defer go-live until a further UAT cycle meets the exit criteria
options.D: Go live on schedule, moving failed cases to Phase 2

questions.key_concept: UAT exit criteria decide go-live readiness; the auditor recommends meeting them, with any deviation formally documented by the steering committee.
questions.pre_read: Compare the pass rate with the agreed criteria. Ask which option keeps the criteria meaningful and the auditor independent.
questions.correct_explanation: Agreed exit criteria are the control that decides readiness. With fewer than half the cases passed, the auditor should recommend deferring go-live until a further cycle meets them, with any deviation formally documented by the steering committee. Phase 2 deferral is the runner-up: it meets the date, but it accepts large untested risk without meeting the agreed criteria.

wrong_explanations.A: Removing failing cases hides the problem and makes the exit criteria meaningless. It defeats the control.
wrong_explanations.B: Executing tests is management's job. Audit performing them would impair independence and not fix the defects.
wrong_explanations.D: Going live with most cases unpassed shifts major untested risk into production and overrides the agreed criteria under schedule pressure.

tips: Eliminate: A manipulates the scope to fake a pass, and B has the auditor perform management's testing.
Final two: C beats D because agreed exit criteria should decide readiness; going live on schedule accepts major untested risk.
Exam cue: when testing fails its exit criteria, the auditor recommends holding to the criteria and documenting any deviation.

questions.question: Hours before branches open, a core-banking cutover shows an unexplained $4.7M deposit variance; a tested fallback plan exists. What is the IS auditor's BEST advice?

options.A: Invoke the fallback plan and revert to the legacy system
options.B: Lock the affected accounts and open on the new platform
options.C: Post the variance to suspense and reconcile at month-end
options.D: Open on the new platform and investigate using live data

questions.key_concept: When cutover reconciliation shows an unexplained material variance, invoking the tested fallback plan protects data integrity and customers.
questions.pre_read: Note that the cause is unknown. Ask which option avoids relying on any data from the new platform.
questions.correct_explanation: A material variance with an unknown cause means the integrity of the new platform's balances cannot be trusted. The documented, tested fallback exists for exactly this situation. Locking affected accounts is the runner-up: it contains part of the exposure, but with the root cause unknown the auditor cannot be sure other accounts are correct.

wrong_explanations.B: Locking only the visibly affected accounts assumes the problem is contained. With the root cause unknown, other balances may also be wrong.
wrong_explanations.C: Clearing an unexplained variance to suspense hides an integrity failure. It also delays resolution until month-end.
wrong_explanations.D: Investigating with live transactions compounds bad balances and puts customers' funds at risk while the cause is unknown.

tips: Eliminate: C hides the variance in a suspense account, and D lets customers transact on untrusted data.
Final two: A beats B because with the root cause unknown, only fallback protects all balances; locking assumes the problem is contained.
Exam cue: an unexplained material conversion variance plus a tested fallback means revert, not patch and proceed.

questions.subtopic: Major Release Governance Under Regulatory Deadline
questions.question: A release must meet a fixed regulatory deadline in five weeks, but two of nine new reports, neither required by the regulation, remain blocked in UAT. What should the IS auditor MOST appropriately recommend?

options.A: Deploy everything, excluding the blocked reports from UAT scope
options.B: Ship a tested subset; defer blocked reports under risk acceptance
options.C: Adopt manual workarounds for the blocked reports as permanent controls
options.D: Halt the entire release until both blocked reports pass UAT

questions.key_concept: Under fixed deadlines, ship a fully tested scope subset and defer blocked items with documented risk acceptance; never skip testing silently.
questions.pre_read: Notice the deadline is fixed and only part of the scope is blocked. Ask which option keeps testing intact and still meets the date.
questions.correct_explanation: Splitting scope lets the organization meet the regulatory deadline with a subset that has fully passed UAT, while the blocked reports follow in a later release under formally documented risk acceptance. Halting everything is the runner-up: it protects quality, but it guarantees a missed fixed deadline when a fully tested subset could ship safely.

wrong_explanations.A: Silently dropping blocked items from test scope ships untested code and hides the gap from decision-makers.
wrong_explanations.C: Workarounds can bridge a short gap, but making them permanent replaces a designed control with an informal one.
wrong_explanations.D: Holding the whole release forfeits the regulatory deadline even though most reports could ship fully tested.

tips: Eliminate: A ships untested code without disclosure, and C turns a temporary workaround into a permanent control.
Final two: B beats D because a fully tested subset meets the deadline with documented risk; halting everything misses it needlessly.
Exam cue: under a fixed deadline, reduce scope to what is fully tested and formally accept the residual risk, rather than skip testing.

questions.subtopic: Project Management Structures. Projectized vs Functional vs Matrix
questions.question: In a projectized organization, a developer must be moved to a critical project task. Who has the PRIMARY authority to make this reassignment?

options.A: The developer's functional department manager
options.B: The vendor account manager under the outsourcing contract
options.C: The project manager leading the project team
options.D: The project sponsor who signed the project charter

questions.key_concept: In a projectized structure, team members report to the project manager, who has full authority over project resources.
questions.pre_read: Recall how authority differs across functional, matrix and projectized structures. Then separate sponsor duties from day-to-day control.
questions.correct_explanation: In a projectized structure, staff report directly to the project manager for the life of the project, and the project manager has full authority over those resources. The sponsor is the runner-up: the sponsor authorizes the project and handles escalations, but day-to-day assignment of team members is delegated to the project manager.

wrong_explanations.A: Functional managers control staff in functional and matrix structures. In a projectized structure, staff report to the project manager.
wrong_explanations.B: Vendor managers control outsourced staff. Nothing in the stem suggests the developer is contracted.
wrong_explanations.D: The sponsor authorizes the project and resolves escalations. Routine task assignment is delegated to the project manager.

tips: Eliminate: A describes functional or matrix authority, and B applies only to outsourced staff.
Final two: C beats D because projectized structures give the project manager full resource authority; the sponsor handles escalations, not assignments.
Exam cue: projectized means the project manager controls resources; functional means department managers do; matrix splits authority.

questions.question: An IS auditor finds that orders with invalid customer IDs are reaching an order system's processing batches. Which control is MOST likely missing?

options.A: Run-to-run totals between processing steps
options.B: Controlled distribution of output reports to recipients
options.C: Sign-on authentication of order-entry users
options.D: Field validity checks at data entry

questions.key_concept: Input controls validate that data is complete, accurate, valid and authorized before processing; processing, output and access controls serve other purposes.
questions.pre_read: Locate where the failure started. Ask which control category acts at that point in the data flow.
questions.correct_explanation: Input controls check that data is complete, accurate, valid and authorized before it is processed. Invalid IDs reaching processing means validity checks at entry are absent or failing. Run-to-run totals are the runner-up: they protect processing integrity, but they only confirm that records pass between steps unchanged, so invalid records flow through with totals intact.

wrong_explanations.A: Run-to-run totals detect lost or altered records between steps. They do not judge whether a record's contents are valid.
wrong_explanations.B: Output distribution controls who receives reports. It acts after processing and cannot stop invalid input.
wrong_explanations.C: Authentication confirms who is entering data, not whether the data entered is valid.

tips: Eliminate: B is an output control, and C is an access control; neither validates the data itself.
Final two: D beats A because validity checks stop bad data at entry; run-to-run totals only confirm records moved intact.
Exam cue: map the failure to the control category: bad data getting in points to input controls such as validity checks.

questions.question: An IS auditor is assessing how quickly a software vendor can tell customers which products contain a newly disclosed library vulnerability. Which vendor artifact BEST supports this?

options.A: A license fee schedule for each bundled third-party component
options.B: A software bill of materials listing each component and version
options.C: An inventory of the vendor's production servers and network devices
options.D: Quarterly vulnerability scan reports for the vendor's hosting servers

questions.key_concept: An SBOM records each product's components, versions and dependencies so a vulnerable component can be traced to affected products quickly.
questions.pre_read: Ask which artifact links a component to the products that contain it, not which one finds weaknesses on servers.
questions.correct_explanation: An SBOM is a formal, machine-readable record of the components and versions in each product, so the vendor can query it and name affected releases within hours. Host vulnerability scans find weaknesses on the vendor's own servers, but they do not reliably reveal libraries embedded inside shipped products, so they cannot show which customer releases are exposed.

wrong_explanations.A: A fee schedule supports license cost tracking. It may name some components but carries no version data to match against a vulnerability.
wrong_explanations.C: A hardware inventory covers physical assets, not the software components built into a product.
wrong_explanations.D: Host scans assess the vendor's own infrastructure. They do not inventory libraries compiled into products shipped to customers.

tips: Eliminate: A tracks license fees, not versions, and C inventories hardware, not software components.
Final two: B beats D because an SBOM maps components to products, while host scans only check the vendor's own servers.
Exam cue: 'which products contain component X' is exactly the question an SBOM exists to answer.

questions.question: In a design review, an IS auditor finds that users could later deny approving a payment because the system keeps no reliable record of actions. Which STRIDE category and control fit BEST?

options.A: Information disclosure, mitigated by encrypting approval records
options.B: Spoofing, mitigated by stronger user authentication at each sign-in
options.C: Repudiation, mitigated by tamper-evident logging of each approval
options.D: Denial of service, mitigated by rate-limiting approval requests

questions.key_concept: STRIDE's Repudiation covers actions users can deny; tamper-evident logs tied to authenticated identities provide non-repudiation.
questions.pre_read: Recall the six STRIDE letters, then match the threat to the property lost: identity, integrity, accountability, confidentiality, availability or authorization.
questions.correct_explanation: Repudiation is the threat that a user can deny an action and the system cannot prove otherwise. The fitting control is tamper-evident logging that ties each approval to an authenticated identity. Spoofing is the runner-up: stronger authentication confirms who signs in, but without a protected record of each action the user can still dispute the approval.

wrong_explanations.A: Disclosure concerns data leaking to unauthorized parties. The finding is about proving who acted, not about confidentiality.
wrong_explanations.B: Spoofing is impersonating another identity. Stronger authentication helps, but without a protected action record the approval can still be disputed.
wrong_explanations.D: Denial of service concerns availability. 'Deny' in the stem means disputing an action, not blocking service.

tips: Eliminate: A addresses confidentiality and D addresses availability; neither concerns proving who approved.
Final two: C beats B because the gap is evidence of the action, which logging supplies; authentication alone proves only who signed in.
Exam cue: 'the user denies doing it and nothing proves otherwise' maps to Repudiation; the fix is accountable, tamper-evident logging.

questions.question: A project steering committee will decide on a major ERP investment using a feasibility study that covers only technical and economic factors. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Approve the investment, since economic feasibility subsumes other factors
options.B: Commission an independent validation of the cost-benefit figures
options.C: Approve now and assess the remaining factors during design
options.D: Extend the study to operational, legal and schedule feasibility

questions.key_concept: A complete feasibility study covers technical, economic, legal, operational and schedule dimensions before the go/no-go decision.
questions.pre_read: Count which feasibility dimensions are missing, then ask whether the fix belongs before or after approval.
questions.correct_explanation: A go/no-go decision needs every feasibility dimension: technical, economic, operational, legal and schedule. Any one of them can sink a technically sound, profitable project, so the gaps should be closed before approval. Validating the cost-benefit figures improves a dimension already covered, but leaves operational, legal and schedule risks unexamined when the committee decides.

wrong_explanations.A: Economic viability does not show that users can operate the system, that it is lawful, or that it can be delivered in time.
wrong_explanations.B: Better cost figures strengthen a dimension already studied. The committee would still decide without operational, legal and schedule evidence.
wrong_explanations.C: Feasibility informs the approval decision. Studying missing dimensions after approval commits funds before the risks are known.

tips: Eliminate: A assumes cost covers every other risk, and C studies feasibility after the decision it should inform.
Final two: D beats B because the gap is missing dimensions; refining cost figures leaves operational, legal and schedule blind spots.
Exam cue: close feasibility gaps before approval, and remember TELOS: technical, economic, legal, operational, schedule.

questions.question: An IS auditor reviews how a PMO compares development productivity across teams using Java, COBOL and a low-code platform. Which sizing measure is MOST appropriate?

options.A: Function points counted from user-visible functional requirements
options.B: Story points estimated by each team during sprint planning
options.C: Lines of code delivered per developer each month
options.D: Number of source files committed in each release

questions.key_concept: Function point analysis sizes software by delivered functionality, making it language-independent and usable for cross-platform comparison and early estimates.
questions.pre_read: Note the mixed technologies. Ask which measure stays comparable when languages and teams differ.
questions.correct_explanation: Function points measure functional size from what users see, independent of language, so Java, COBOL and low-code teams can be compared on the same scale. Story points are useful for a team's own planning, but each team calibrates them differently, so they cannot support cross-team productivity comparisons.

wrong_explanations.B: Story points are relative to each team's own calibration. A point in one team does not equal a point in another.
wrong_explanations.C: Lines of code depend on language; COBOL and low-code platforms produce very different counts for the same function.
wrong_explanations.D: File counts reflect how code is organized, not delivered functionality, and vary widely across languages and platforms.

tips: Eliminate: C and D count code artifacts, which vary by language and platform for the same function.
Final two: A beats B because function points follow a standard counting method, while story points are calibrated differently by each team.
Exam cue: comparing across languages, or sizing before code exists, points to function point analysis.

questions.question: An IS auditor reviews a support team that handles an unpredictable stream of incidents and small changes whose priorities shift daily. Which delivery method is the MOST suitable fit?

options.A: Waterfall, with stage-gate sign-off on small changes
options.B: Kanban, with work-in-progress limits and pull-based flow
options.C: Scrum, with fixed two-week sprints and sprint commitments
options.D: A V-model, with formal verification at each phase

questions.key_concept: Kanban fits continuous, variable-priority work through pull-based flow and WIP limits; Scrum fits time-boxed iterative product development.
questions.pre_read: Look at how the work arrives. Batched, plannable work suits sprints; an unpredictable stream suits flow.
questions.correct_explanation: Kanban suits work that arrives continuously with changing priorities: items are pulled when capacity frees up, and work-in-progress limits expose bottlenecks. Scrum is the runner-up, but its fixed sprint commitments assume work can be planned in batches; daily priority shifts would keep breaking the sprint or force urgent incidents to wait.

wrong_explanations.A: Stage gates suit large, defined projects. Applying sign-off gates to each small change slows urgent support work.
wrong_explanations.C: Sprints assume work can be committed in batches. Daily priority changes would keep disrupting commitments or delay urgent incidents.
wrong_explanations.D: The V-model pairs each development phase with a test phase. It suits planned builds, not a support queue.

tips: Eliminate: A and D are plan-driven models built for defined projects, not an unpredictable support queue.
Final two: B beats C because pull-based flow absorbs daily priority shifts, while sprint commitments assume work can be planned in batches.
Exam cue: continuous, interrupt-driven work points to Kanban; time-boxed product development points to Scrum.

questions.question: An IS auditor finds that pipeline scan findings sit unresolved for months because the security team logs them but developers never see them. Which change BEST reflects DevSecOps practice?

options.A: Have the security team fix findings in a central queue
options.B: Turn off the scan rules that produce the most findings
options.C: Feed findings into team backlogs with severity-based fix deadlines
options.D: Commission an annual penetration test to confirm which findings matter

questions.key_concept: DevSecOps makes security a shared responsibility: scan findings go into delivery teams' backlogs with severity-based fix deadlines.
questions.pre_read: Ask who owns a security finding in DevSecOps, and how it reaches the people who can fix it.
questions.correct_explanation: DevSecOps makes security a shared responsibility: findings flow into the delivery team's own backlog, are prioritized like other work and must be fixed within severity-based deadlines, so the people who wrote the code fix it. Central fixing by the security team is the runner-up: it gets findings addressed, but it keeps security outside the team, creates a bottleneck and leaves developers repeating the same flaws.

wrong_explanations.A: A central fixing team becomes a bottleneck and keeps developers unaware of their own flaws, so the same weaknesses keep recurring.
wrong_explanations.B: Silencing noisy rules hides risk instead of treating it. Tuning false positives is valid, but disabling rules by volume is not.
wrong_explanations.D: An annual test is periodic and late. It does not change who owns findings or how quickly they are fixed.

tips: Eliminate: B hides risk by silencing scan rules, and D adds a late, periodic test that does not change ownership.
Final two: C beats A because DevSecOps makes the delivery team own and fix its flaws, rather than routing them to a central bottleneck.
Exam cue: in DevSecOps questions, prefer the option that puts security work inside the team's normal workflow.

questions.question: Before UAT starts on a new billing system, an IS auditor reviews the acceptance criteria. Which attribute provides the MOST assurance that the criteria are well formed?

options.A: Measurable criteria agreed by the business owner before testing
options.B: Criteria approved by QA and traced to the detailed technical design
options.C: Criteria drafted by developers from their own build decisions
options.D: Code-coverage and unit-test pass rates used as exit thresholds

questions.key_concept: Well-formed UAT criteria are measurable, tied to business requirements, agreed by the business owner and fixed before testing starts.
questions.pre_read: Ask who owns acceptance and what the system is being tested against: business requirements or the technical build.
questions.correct_explanation: UAT confirms the system meets business needs, so its criteria must be measurable, agreed by the business owner and fixed before testing begins. QA approval with traceability to the technical design is the runner-up: it shows rigour, but it validates against how the system was built rather than what the business required, and the business owner has not accepted the criteria.

wrong_explanations.B: Tracing to the technical design tests what was built, not what the business needs. Without business-owner agreement, acceptance lacks its proper owner.
wrong_explanations.C: Developers defining criteria from their own build choices removes independence; the system is judged against itself.
wrong_explanations.D: Coverage and unit-test rates measure developer testing. They say nothing about whether business requirements are met.

tips: Eliminate: C lets the builders judge their own work, and D applies developer-testing metrics to a business test.
Final two: A beats B because acceptance belongs to the business owner against requirements; QA tracing to design checks what was built.
Exam cue: UAT criteria are business-owned, testable and set before execution; design- or code-based criteria are the wrong test level.

questions.question: A QA manager reports 95% code coverage on a payments module, yet defects keep reaching production. Which technique BEST measures how well the test suite detects faults?

options.A: Raising the coverage target to 100 percent of statements
options.B: Static code analysis on every pull request
options.C: Load testing at projected peak transaction volumes
options.D: Mutation testing that injects small faults into the code

questions.key_concept: Mutation testing measures test-suite effectiveness by checking whether tests catch deliberately injected faults; coverage only shows what code ran.
questions.pre_read: Separate 'code was executed' from 'a fault would be detected'. Ask which technique measures the second.
questions.correct_explanation: Mutation testing seeds small deliberate faults into the code and checks whether the existing tests fail. The share of mutants caught measures the suite's ability to detect defects. Raising coverage is the runner-up, but coverage only shows which lines ran; tests can execute every line with weak assertions and still miss the faults that reach production.

wrong_explanations.A: More coverage shows more lines executed, not that tests check results. High coverage with weak assertions already explains the escaping defects.
wrong_explanations.B: Static analysis inspects the code for flaws. It does not measure whether the test suite would catch them.
wrong_explanations.C: Load testing checks performance under volume. It does not evaluate the fault-detecting power of the test suite.

tips: Eliminate: B inspects code rather than tests, and C measures performance, not fault detection.
Final two: D beats A because mutation scores show whether tests catch faults, while coverage only shows which lines ran.
Exam cue: high coverage plus escaped defects signals weak assertions; mutation testing measures what the tests actually verify.

questions.subtopic: DAST vs IAST vs RASP. Differentiation
questions.question: A bank wants its customer web application to detect and block attacks from inside the running code in production. Which control should the IS auditor expect as the BEST fit?

options.A: Static application security testing of source code at each commit
options.B: Runtime application self-protection within the live application
options.C: Interactive application security testing during QA test runs
options.D: Dynamic application security testing scans before each release

questions.key_concept: DAST tests a running app externally, IAST instruments it during testing, and RASP protects it from inside in production.
questions.pre_read: Note two clues: inside the code, and in production. Ask which tool blocks attacks rather than only finding weaknesses.
questions.correct_explanation: Runtime application self-protection (RASP) runs inside the production application, sees how each request is actually handled and can block an attack as it happens. Interactive testing (IAST) also instruments the running code, which makes it the runner-up, but it runs in test environments to find vulnerabilities before release; it does not protect live traffic.

wrong_explanations.A: SAST analyses source code before it runs. It finds coding flaws early but cannot see or block live attacks.
wrong_explanations.C: IAST instruments the application during QA testing to find vulnerabilities. It is a pre-release testing tool, not production protection.
wrong_explanations.D: DAST probes a running application from outside, usually before release. It reports weaknesses but does not block attacks in production.

tips: Eliminate: A reads code that is not running, and D tests from outside without blocking anything.
Final two: B beats C because RASP protects live traffic in production, while IAST instruments the code only during testing.
Exam cue: DAST tests from outside, IAST tests from inside, and RASP protects from inside in production.

questions.question: A development manager wants continuous integration with several production releases each week. Which branching approach should the IS auditor regard as MOST appropriate?

options.A: Short-lived branches merged to trunk daily after automated checks
options.B: Git Flow, with separate develop and release branches per deployment
options.C: Direct commits to the main branch without pull-request review
options.D: Long-lived feature branches merged at the end of each quarter

questions.key_concept: Trunk-based development, with short-lived branches merged daily through checked pull requests, supports continuous integration and frequent releases.
questions.pre_read: Ask how often each approach integrates code, and whether it keeps review and automated testing in place.
questions.correct_explanation: Continuous integration means integrating everyone's work at least daily. Short-lived branches merged to trunk through pull requests with automated checks keep integration frequent while preserving review and testing. Git Flow is the runner-up: it provides structure, but its long-running develop and release branches delay integration and add merge overhead that slows frequent production releases.

wrong_explanations.B: Git Flow's develop and release branches suit scheduled releases. They delay integration and add merge overhead for teams releasing several times a week.
wrong_explanations.C: Committing straight to main integrates often but drops peer review and pre-merge testing, weakening change control.
wrong_explanations.D: Branches kept for months accumulate merge conflicts and defer integration, the opposite of continuous integration.

tips: Eliminate: C removes review and testing, and D defers integration for months.
Final two: A beats B because trunk-based merges integrate daily with checks, while Git Flow's long-running branches delay integration.
Exam cue: continuous integration plus frequent releases points to trunk-based development with gated pull requests.

questions.question: An IS auditor must confirm that only container images built by the organization's own pipeline run in production. Which control provides the BEST assurance?

options.A: Weekly antivirus scans of images running in production
options.B: TLS encryption on every connection to the image registry
options.C: Deployments restricted to a single approved private registry
options.D: Image signing at build, with signature checks before deployment

questions.key_concept: Signing images at build and verifying signatures before deployment proves an image's origin and that it was not altered.
questions.pre_read: Ask which control proves who built the image, rather than where it is stored or how it travels.
questions.correct_explanation: Signing each image in the build pipeline and having the cluster verify the signature before scheduling proves both who built the image and that it has not changed since. Restricting pulls to one approved registry is the runner-up: it narrows the source, but anyone able to push to that registry could place an altered image there.

wrong_explanations.A: Antivirus finds known malware. It cannot show where an image was built or detect subtle unauthorized changes.
wrong_explanations.B: TLS protects images in transit. It does not prove who built the image or that it was unaltered at the source.
wrong_explanations.C: A single registry narrows the source, but an image pushed there through a compromised account would still deploy unverified.

tips: Eliminate: A detects only known malware, and B protects the connection, not the image itself.
Final two: D beats C because a verified signature proves origin and integrity, while a trusted registry only trusts a storage location.
Exam cue: provenance questions want cryptographic signing at build plus verification at deployment.

questions.question: Cloud infrastructure is managed through Infrastructure-as-Code, but engineers can still change settings in the console. Which control should the IS auditor consider MOST effective at detecting unauthorized changes?

options.A: Monthly configuration exports stored offsite for recovery
options.B: Automated policy checks run on every IaC template change
options.C: Continuous comparison of live settings with the IaC definitions
options.D: Annual architecture review of settings against approved baselines

questions.key_concept: IaC drift detection continuously reconciles live cloud state with declared code and alerts on divergence, catching out-of-band changes.
questions.pre_read: Note the console path that bypasses code. Ask which control would still see a change made that way.
questions.correct_explanation: Drift detection continuously compares the live cloud state with the state declared in code and alerts on any difference, so a console change made outside the pipeline is caught quickly. Automated policy checks on IaC templates are the runner-up: they are a strong preventive control, but console changes bypass the templates entirely, so the checks never see them.

wrong_explanations.A: Configuration exports support recovery after an incident. They do not compare states or alert anyone to an unauthorized change.
wrong_explanations.B: Policy checks prevent bad template changes, but console changes never pass through the templates, so the checks cannot detect them.
wrong_explanations.D: An annual review is far too infrequent. Unauthorized changes could persist for months before anyone notices.

tips: Eliminate: A is a recovery measure, and D is too infrequent to detect changes in time.
Final two: C beats B because console changes bypass template checks; only comparing live state with code reveals them.
Exam cue: when changes can bypass the pipeline, choose a detective control that reconciles actual state with the approved baseline.

questions.question: Halfway through the quarter, a product team has used its entire error budget for a customer-facing service. Which response should the IS auditor expect management to take FIRST?

options.A: Lower the SLO target so the budget becomes available again
options.B: Freeze non-essential releases and prioritize reliability work
options.C: Keep releasing, using canary rollouts and extra production monitoring
options.D: Continue normal releases, since features outweigh the SLO

questions.key_concept: When an error budget is exhausted, non-essential releases stop and reliability work takes priority until the budget recovers.
questions.pre_read: Recall what an error budget is for: it decides when the team may keep shipping features and when it must stop.
questions.correct_explanation: An exhausted error budget means users have already absorbed the agreed amount of unreliability. The agreed policy response is to freeze non-essential changes and spend engineering effort on reliability until the budget recovers. Canary rollouts with extra monitoring reduce the risk of each release, but they still spend reliability the service no longer has and sidestep the agreed policy.

wrong_explanations.A: Loosening the target after missing it removes accountability and hides the reliability problem users are already experiencing.
wrong_explanations.C: Safer rollout methods reduce per-release risk but still add change to a service that has used up its tolerance for failure.
wrong_explanations.D: Ignoring the exhausted budget defeats the purpose of setting an SLO and an agreed error-budget policy.

tips: Eliminate: A moves the target after missing it, and D ignores the agreed SLO altogether.
Final two: B beats C because the policy for an exhausted budget is to stop non-essential change, not to release more carefully.
Exam cue: once the error budget is spent, feature releases pause and reliability work takes priority until it recovers.

questions.question: A bank will replace its core platform across six business units with very different processes. Which cutover approach should the IS auditor consider BEST?

options.A: Phased rollout by unit, limiting impact and allowing correction
options.B: Big-bang cutover over one weekend, avoiding temporary interfaces
options.C: Indefinite parallel running of both systems in every unit
options.D: Big-bang cutover scheduled for the quarter-end closing weekend

questions.key_concept: Phased cutover suits complex, multi-unit replacements because staged waves limit blast radius and allow mid-course correction.
questions.pre_read: Weigh complexity and impact. Ask how many units a single failure would hit under each approach.
questions.correct_explanation: With six units and very different processes, a phased rollout limits the blast radius of any failure to one unit and lets lessons from early waves correct later ones. A single big-bang weekend avoids temporary interfaces between old and new systems, but it exposes every unit at once, with no chance to correct course before the whole bank is affected.

wrong_explanations.B: Big-bang suits simpler, lower-risk replacements. Here a single failure would hit all six units at once with no chance to adjust.
wrong_explanations.C: Parallel running is a time-limited validation step. Running both systems indefinitely doubles effort and never completes the transition.
wrong_explanations.D: Quarter-end is a bank's busiest, highest-risk period. A full cutover then compounds migration risk with closing pressure.

tips: Eliminate: C never completes the transition, and D stacks cutover on the riskiest weekend of the quarter.
Final two: A beats B because staged waves contain failures and allow correction; big-bang is simpler but exposes every unit at once.
Exam cue: complex, multi-unit, high-impact replacements point to phased cutover; small, low-risk systems suit big-bang.

questions.question: At month 8 of a 14-month ERP project, the PMO reports a cumulative CPI of 0.78 and SPI of 0.85; the team says recent re-baselining will fix this. What should the IS auditor conclude FIRST?

options.A: Performance is within tolerance for a complex ERP rollout
options.B: A conclusion should wait until re-baselined figures mature
options.C: EVM cannot yet predict outcomes at this stage of a project
options.D: Cost and schedule are materially behind and need corrective action

questions.key_concept: Cumulative CPI and SPI well below 1.0 at mid-project signal material variance that rarely self-corrects and needs corrective action.
questions.pre_read: Read each index against 1.0, then ask whether re-baselining changes performance or only the plan it is measured against.
questions.correct_explanation: Cumulative indices of 0.78 and 0.85 at month 8 mean the project earns 78 cents of value per dollar spent and is 15% behind plan; cumulative CPI rarely recovers much after mid-project. The auditor should report a material variance needing action. Waiting for re-baselined data sounds prudent, but re-baselining resets the yardstick without fixing performance and delays the decision.

wrong_explanations.A: A CPI of 0.78 is well below accepted tolerance. Calling it normal for ERP hides a material overrun.
wrong_explanations.B: Re-baselining changes the plan, not the performance. Waiting delays corrective action while costs keep overrunning.
wrong_explanations.C: By mid-project, cumulative EVM indices are reliable predictors; cumulative CPI tends to stabilize early.

tips: Eliminate: A treats earning only 78 cents of value per dollar spent as normal, and C wrongly claims EVM has no predictive value at mid-project.
Final two: D beats B because re-baselining resets the yardstick but does not fix performance; waiting only delays corrective action.
Exam cue: CPI or SPI well below 1.0 past the midpoint signals real variance; 'it will recover' is a claim, not evidence.

questions.question: A fraud-detection model's false-positive rate has risen from 4% to 11% in eight months, with no retraining or assigned model owner. What should the IS auditor recommend as the BEST response?

options.A: Decommission the model and return to fully manual claim reviews
options.B: Raise the alert threshold to cut false positives now
options.C: Assign an owner and set drift alerts and retraining triggers
options.D: Accept the rate, as it is typical for fraud-detection models

questions.key_concept: Production ML needs lifecycle governance: an accountable owner, drift monitoring, retraining triggers and performance gates.
questions.pre_read: Separate the symptom (rising errors) from the cause (no monitoring or owner). Ask which option fixes the cause.
questions.correct_explanation: The rising false-positive rate is a symptom; the root cause is the absence of lifecycle governance. An accountable owner, drift monitoring with thresholds, and defined retraining and performance gates keep the model reliable over time. Raising the alert threshold is the runner-up: it cuts false positives quickly, but it trades them for missed fraud and leaves the unowned model drifting.

wrong_explanations.A: Decommissioning discards a fixable model and returns to costly manual review, without addressing why degradation went unnoticed.
wrong_explanations.B: A higher threshold cuts false positives but lets more fraud through. With no owner or monitoring, the model keeps drifting unnoticed.
wrong_explanations.D: Accepting a near-tripling of false positives ignores the drift evidence and the missing governance behind it.

tips: Eliminate: A abandons a fixable model, and D accepts degradation as normal.
Final two: C beats B because governance fixes the root cause, while tuning the threshold only shifts today's symptom.
Exam cue: when a symptom comes with a missing control framework, recommend the framework, not the one-time fix.

questions.subtopic: Open-Source License Risk. Strong Copyleft (GPL) in SaaS
questions.question: Before investor due diligence, an IS auditor finds core SaaS modules import an AGPL-licensed library; the CTO and legal counsel disagree on its obligations. What should the auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Isolate copyleft code and scan licenses before merging
options.B: Obtain a documented legal opinion on the library's obligations
options.C: Rewrite every open-source module using proprietary code
options.D: Leave the decision to the investor's risk appetite

questions.key_concept: Open-source license risk is managed by tracking licenses, scanning before merge and isolating strong-copyleft components.
questions.pre_read: Notice the disagreement between experts. Ask which option stays safe whichever interpretation turns out to be right.
questions.correct_explanation: When experts disagree on a license obligation, the sound response reduces exposure under either reading. Isolating the copyleft component behind a service boundary and scanning licenses before code is merged does that, and stops new issues entering. A documented legal opinion is the runner-up, but it bets the product on one contested interpretation and adds no ongoing control.

wrong_explanations.B: A legal opinion records one contested view of one library. If that view is wrong, the exposure remains, and no ongoing control is added.
wrong_explanations.C: Rewriting all open-source code is costly and unnecessary; most permissive-licensed dependencies carry no comparable obligation.
wrong_explanations.D: License compliance is the organization's own responsibility. Deferring to an investor's appetite abdicates control of the risk.

tips: Eliminate: C overreacts by discarding all open source, and D hands the organization's risk to an outsider.
Final two: A beats B because isolation and scanning reduce exposure whichever legal view prevails; an opinion only bets on one view.
Exam cue: when experts disagree on an obligation, prefer the control that reduces exposure under either interpretation.

questions.question: Twelve weeks before a payments-platform cutover, the CIO plans one technical-only mock conversion three weeks before go-live. What should the IS auditor recommend to the cutover risk committee as BEST?

options.A: One full end-to-end rehearsal in the final week before go-live
options.B: Staged rehearsals adding business steps, each reviewed before the next
options.C: Rely on the documented playbook, since rehearsal repeats steps already known
options.D: Run the technical rehearsal and test business steps after go-live

questions.key_concept: High-stakes cutovers need staged rehearsals covering technical and business steps, each reviewed, with time left to fix issues.
questions.pre_read: Check two things: does the rehearsal cover business steps, and is there time to fix what it finds?
questions.correct_explanation: A high-volume payments cutover needs rehearsals that cover technical and business procedures and leave time to fix what they reveal. Staged cycles, technical first, then end-to-end with business teams, then a dry run, each followed by a review, achieve that. One full rehearsal a week out is realistic, but any serious issue it finds leaves no time to correct.

wrong_explanations.A: A single late rehearsal tests the right scope, but leaves no time to fix problems before go-live.
wrong_explanations.C: A playbook that has never been exercised is unproven. Rehearsals find gaps in timing, hand-offs and procedures that documents hide.
wrong_explanations.D: Testing business procedures after go-live exposes live payments to untested operational steps during the riskiest period.

tips: Eliminate: C trusts an unexercised playbook, and D leaves business procedures untested until after go-live.
Final two: B beats A because staged cycles leave time to fix what each rehearsal finds; one late rehearsal leaves none.
