questions.question: An organization plans to start chaos engineering experiments in production. Which condition should the IS auditor consider MOST important before experiments begin?

options.A: A stated hypothesis, blast-radius limits and automatic abort criteria
options.B: Unannounced random failures to test staff responsiveness
options.C: A rule that experiments may cause no service disruption
options.D: Change-board approval for each scheduled experiment in advance

questions.key_concept: Chaos engineering runs controlled experiments: a hypothesis, blast-radius limits, automatic abort and captured learning.
questions.pre_read: Ask which condition would actually limit the damage if an experiment goes wrong.
questions.correct_explanation: Chaos engineering is controlled experimentation, not random breakage. Each experiment needs a hypothesis about steady-state behaviour, limits on how much of the service it can affect, and criteria that stop it automatically if metrics breach thresholds. Change-board approval adds oversight, but approval alone does not contain the harm once an experiment misbehaves; the built-in limits and abort criteria do.

wrong_explanations.B: Random, unannounced failures without hypothesis or limits are uncontrolled outages, not engineering experiments.
wrong_explanations.C: Experiments deliberately introduce failure; a no-disruption rule makes them impossible rather than safe.
wrong_explanations.D: Approval is useful oversight, but it does not limit impact or stop an experiment that starts causing harm.

tips: Eliminate: B is an uncontrolled outage, and C rules out the practice itself.
Final two: A beats D because built-in impact limits and abort criteria contain harm; approval alone does not.
Exam cue: for any planned production risk, look for a hypothesis, defined scope and stop criteria before sign-off.

questions.question: An IS auditor must confirm that a microservices platform can explain why individual customer requests run slowly. Which telemetry is MOST important to verify?

options.A: Correlated logs, metrics and traces sharing one request ID
options.B: Centralized application logs from every service, retained for one year
options.C: Source code, build artifacts and runtime configuration files
options.D: Static-analysis results and unit-test coverage from recent builds

questions.key_concept: Observability rests on logs, metrics and traces correlated by shared request context, so one request can be followed across services.
questions.pre_read: Notice the stem asks about individual requests across many services. Ask which evidence can follow one request end to end.
questions.correct_explanation: A slow request crosses many services, so diagnosing it needs all three signals tied together: metrics show that latency rose, traces show which service hop was slow, and logs explain why. A shared request ID links them. Centralized logs alone are useful, but each service logs in isolation, so the auditor cannot reconstruct one request's path across the platform.

wrong_explanations.B: Per-service logs without traces or a shared request context cannot show which hop in a cross-service request caused the delay.
wrong_explanations.C: Code and configuration describe how the system is built, not how it behaves at runtime, so they cannot explain live latency.
wrong_explanations.D: Build-time quality results show code quality before release; they produce no runtime evidence about production request behavior.

tips: Eliminate: C and D are build-time artifacts, so neither shows how live requests behave in production.
Final two: A beats B because only correlated traces, metrics and logs can follow one request across services; isolated logs cannot.
Exam cue: for distributed systems, look for correlation across signals, not just more retention of a single signal.

questions.question: An IS auditor finds application API keys and database credentials unchanged for three years, and no record of which systems use each one. What should the auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Rotate the credentials only after a confirmed breach occurs
options.B: Rotate every credential at once in one change window
options.C: Map each secret to its owner and consuming services
options.D: Leave the credentials unchanged to avoid deployment outages

questions.key_concept: Safe secrets remediation starts with an inventory of owners and consumers, enabling planned rotation and a move to short-lived vault credentials.
questions.pre_read: Notice nobody knows which systems use each secret. Ask what must be known before any rotation is safe.
questions.correct_explanation: Before secrets can be rotated safely or moved into a vault, the firm must know who owns each one and which services depend on it; otherwise rotation breaks unknown consumers and causes outages. Rotating everything at once tackles three years of exposure directly, but without that map it is likely to fail mid-change and push teams back to static secrets.

wrong_explanations.A: Waiting for a confirmed breach means a stolen secret stays usable until the damage is detected, which may be never.
wrong_explanations.B: Rotating blind breaks consumers nobody has identified, causing outages and pressure to roll back to the old secrets.
wrong_explanations.D: Unchanged credentials give any past leak permanent access. Rotation risk is managed through automation, not by avoiding rotation.

tips: Eliminate: A rotates only after damage is known, and D never rotates, so a leaked secret works indefinitely.
Final two: C beats B because rotation is safe only once owners and consumers are known; blind rotation causes outages.
Exam cue: for long-unmanaged assets, inventory and ownership come before remediation at scale.

questions.question: An IS auditor reviews stored card numbers that the payment service must recover, but copies stolen from other systems must be useless. Which control is BEST?

options.A: Display masking that reveals just the last four digits
options.B: Tokenization using surrogate values mapped in a secured vault
options.C: Field-level encryption of card numbers in each application database
options.D: One-way hashing of card numbers before they are stored

questions.key_concept: Tokenization swaps sensitive data for vault-mapped surrogates; masking hides it for display; encryption is reversible by anyone holding the key.
questions.pre_read: Notice two needs in the stem: the data must be recoverable, and stolen copies must be worthless. Test each option against both.
questions.correct_explanation: Tokenization replaces each card number with a surrogate that has no mathematical link to it; only the vault can map it back, so the payment service can recover the number while tokens stolen elsewhere are worthless. Encryption is reversible too, but encrypted card numbers remain card data: anyone who obtains the key can decrypt them, and every holding system stays in scope.

wrong_explanations.A: Display masking only hides digits on screen or in reports. It is not designed to let the payment service recover the full number.
wrong_explanations.C: Encrypted values are still card data. Systems holding them stay in scope, and a stolen key exposes every value.
wrong_explanations.D: A one-way hash cannot be reversed, so the payment service could not recover the card number it needs.

tips: Eliminate: A and D cannot give the payment service the original card number back.
Final two: B beats C because tokens carry no recoverable data outside the vault, while ciphertext is exposed by any stolen key.
Exam cue: reversible plus useless-if-stolen points to tokenization; masking is for display, encryption keeps data in scope.

questions.question: An IS auditor finds that the IT service catalog lists applications with no named owner and still offers retired services. Which control BEST addresses the cause?

options.A: Allow each team to publish its catalog entries without any central review
options.B: Retire the catalog in favor of team-run self-service portals
options.C: Have the service desk purge stale entries in an annual clean-up
options.D: Require a named owner and a yearly owner review of each entry

questions.key_concept: Service catalog governance needs an accountable owner for each entry who reviews it periodically; a purge by a non-owner leaves the cause.
questions.pre_read: Notice the stem asks for the cause, not a quick fix. Separate options that prevent recurrence from those that clean up later.
questions.correct_explanation: The findings show entries without accountable owners and no review as services change. Requiring a named owner for each entry, who confirms its status in a yearly review, fixes the cause; a catalog changes slowly, so an annual owner review is proportionate. An annual clean-up by the service desk removes stale entries, but the desk does not own the services, so errors return between purges.

wrong_explanations.A: Unreviewed publishing is what lets ownerless and retired entries accumulate; it removes the control rather than adding one.
wrong_explanations.B: Scattering services across team portals removes the single governed view that users and service management rely on.
wrong_explanations.C: A yearly purge treats symptoms after the fact, done by a team that does not own the services, so the gaps recur.

tips: Eliminate: A removes review entirely, and B removes the catalog instead of governing it.
Final two: D beats C because the accountable owner reviews each entry; a service-desk purge cleans up without fixing ownership.
Exam cue: a periodic review is a sound control when the accountable owner performs it and the asset changes slowly.

questions.question: A CIO plans to promote a successful machine-learning proof of concept straight into production, although it has no error handling, monitoring or rollback. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Promote the code now and retrofit controls after go-live
options.B: Cancel the initiative, since proof-of-concept code cannot be salvaged
options.C: Have the data scientist add error handling before go-live
options.D: Require production-readiness criteria and a staged rollout before release

questions.key_concept: A proof of concept must pass production-readiness criteria, including resilience, monitoring, rollback and ownership, before staged release.
questions.pre_read: Notice several missing controls in the stem. Ask which option addresses all of them before go-live.
questions.correct_explanation: A proof of concept shows value in a controlled setting; it is not built for live data, scale or support. Defining production-readiness criteria covering error handling, monitoring, rollback, scaling and team ownership, then rolling out in stages, addresses every gap before release. Adding error handling alone fixes one gap and leaves the sole developer, monitoring and rollback problems unresolved.

wrong_explanations.A: Retrofitting controls after go-live exposes live operations to failures with no monitoring or way back. Controls belong before release.
wrong_explanations.B: The proof of concept showed real value. Gaps in hardening call for productionization, not abandoning a working idea.
wrong_explanations.C: Error handling is one gap of several. Monitoring, rollback, scale and dependence on one person remain unaddressed.

tips: Eliminate: A releases without controls, and B discards a proven idea instead of hardening it.
Final two: D beats C because readiness criteria cover every gap and ownership, while one fix by one person leaves the rest open.
Exam cue: a proof of concept is not production. Expect readiness gates and staged rollout before release.

questions.question: A backdoor is disclosed in an open-source library used by the firm's billing and authentication services. Once the incident is declared, which action should the IS auditor expect FIRST?

options.A: Pin the current library version and freeze further dependency updates
options.B: Scope affected services and contain or remove the compromised library
options.C: Review dependency-selection policy and update the approved library list
options.D: Keep services running while monitoring vulnerability feeds for exploits

questions.key_concept: After a supply-chain compromise, scope the affected systems and contain the component first; policy improvements follow in post-incident review.
questions.pre_read: Notice the word FIRST. Order the options by incident phase: analysis, containment, eradication, recovery, lessons learned.
questions.correct_explanation: Incident handling starts with analysis and containment: identify which services use the library, then contain the exposure by removing or isolating the compromised version, while hunting for signs the backdoor was used. Reviewing the dependency-selection policy is valuable, but it belongs to post-incident lessons learned; doing it first leaves billing and authentication exposed while the policy is debated.

wrong_explanations.A: Pinning freezes the compromised version in place. It blocks new versions but leaves the backdoor running in critical services.
wrong_explanations.C: Policy review is a lessons-learned step after containment. Done first, it leaves the backdoor active in production.
wrong_explanations.D: Monitoring alone does nothing to stop a disclosed backdoor in authentication and billing paths. Containment cannot wait for exploitation.

tips: Eliminate: A and D both leave a known backdoor running in critical services.
Final two: B beats C because containment comes before lessons learned; policy review is right activity, wrong time.
Exam cue: in incident questions asking FIRST, choose scoping and containment before root-cause or policy improvement.

questions.question: A code change let one SaaS customer see another tenant's aggregated metrics for seven hours before rollback. Which response is MOST appropriate for the IS auditor to advise management?

options.A: Invoke breach response, including notification assessment for affected tenants
options.B: Close the incident, since the rollback ended the exposure
options.C: Harden tenant isolation and add regression tests, then close the incident
options.D: Transfer ownership of the whole response to legal counsel

questions.key_concept: A cross-tenant data exposure triggers formal breach response, including scoping and notification assessment, not only a technical fix.
questions.pre_read: Notice that another customer actually saw the data. Ask which option covers obligations to the affected tenant, not just the defect.
questions.correct_explanation: Cross-tenant exposure is a potential data breach, so the formal breach process applies: scope what was seen, assess regulatory and contractual notification duties such as the GDPR 72-hour clock, inform affected customers, find the root cause and fix it. Hardening isolation is a necessary part of that remediation, but closing the incident after a technical fix skips the notification assessment.

wrong_explanations.B: Rollback stops further exposure but does not address data already seen, or the firm's notification and contractual obligations.
wrong_explanations.C: Technical hardening is needed, but closing the incident afterward skips the assessment of notification duties to customers and regulators.
wrong_explanations.D: Legal counsel advises, but scoping, root cause and isolation fixes need security, privacy and technical owners in the response.

tips: Eliminate: B treats rollback as resolution, and D hands a technical incident wholly to lawyers.
Final two: A beats C because a fix without notification assessment leaves legal and customer obligations unmet.
Exam cue: when data crosses a boundary it should not, think breach response with notification analysis, not just a bug fix.

questions.question: Aware since Tuesday 14:00 that EU customer data was exposed internally, the CPO wants to delay any GDPR notification decision until the investigation ends. What is the IS auditor's BEST advice?

options.A: Assess risk now; file one complete notice when facts are confirmed
options.B: Notify US state regulators, since GDPR excludes internal incidents
options.C: Assess the risk now; notify within 72 hours, supplementing later
options.D: Notify every affected data subject before any risk assessment

questions.key_concept: GDPR Article 33 requires risk assessment and authority notification within 72 hours of awareness, with details supplemented as they emerge.
questions.pre_read: Notice when awareness began. Ask whether the legal deadline depends on the investigation finishing.
questions.correct_explanation: Under GDPR Article 33 the 72-hour clock starts at awareness, not at the end of the investigation. The controller should assess the risk to individuals now and, if notification is required, notify the supervisory authority within 72 hours, adding information in phases as Article 33(4) allows. Holding a single complete notice until the facts are confirmed sounds careful but risks missing the legal deadline.

wrong_explanations.A: The deadline runs from awareness. Article 33(4) allows phased information, so holding one notice for confirmed facts risks missing the 72-hour limit.
wrong_explanations.B: GDPR covers personal data breaches whether or not data leaves the organization. US regulators do not replace EU duties.
wrong_explanations.D: Notifying individuals depends on a high-risk finding. Skipping the risk assessment is not the required process and may cause needless alarm.

tips: Eliminate: B misreads GDPR scope, and D skips the risk assessment the regulation requires.
Final two: C beats A because the 72-hour clock runs from awareness and phased notification is allowed.
Exam cue: for GDPR timing, the clock starts at awareness; assess risk now and supplement details later.

questions.question: Three product teams plan to build their own authentication because the shared platform team's backlog blocks their roadmaps. Which governance response should the IS auditor recommend to management as BEST?

options.A: Let each product team build its own authentication service
options.B: Embed platform engineers in product teams and disband the central platform
options.C: Mandate the shared platform and prohibit team-built alternatives
options.D: Fund platform capacity to demand, with cross-team priorities and SLAs

questions.key_concept: Shared platforms need demand-based capacity, transparent cross-team prioritization and service levels to prevent costly fragmentation.
questions.pre_read: Notice why teams want to bypass the platform. Ask which option fixes that reason while keeping one standard.
questions.correct_explanation: The root cause is a shared service without capacity matched to demand or a fair way to rank requests. Funding the platform by demand, prioritizing across teams and committing to service levels, in line with COBIT APO08 and APO09, removes the bottleneck while keeping one standard. Mandating the platform prevents fragmentation, but without capacity the teams stay blocked.

wrong_explanations.A: Separate authentication builds fragment a critical security control, multiplying attack surface and inconsistent standards across the firm.
wrong_explanations.B: Spreading platform engineers across teams breaks up the shared service and leads to divergent authentication designs.
wrong_explanations.C: A mandate stops fragmentation but leaves the capacity shortfall unsolved, so roadmaps stay blocked and pressure to bypass continues.

questions.question: All four engineers who maintain a custom laboratory system resign with nine weeks' notice; replacements need six months to onboard. Which recommendation by the IS auditor BEST reduces the knowledge-loss risk?

options.A: Offer retention bonuses so at least one current engineer stays on
options.B: Document runbooks and record walkthroughs with paired handovers
options.C: Rely on existing documentation and let new hires learn on the job
options.D: Decommission the system before the engineers leave the firm

questions.key_concept: Key-person risk is reduced by capturing knowledge in documentation and handovers, not by relying on retaining individuals.
questions.pre_read: Notice the short notice period. Ask which option makes knowledge independent of any one person.
questions.correct_explanation: Knowledge held only in people's heads leaves with them. Capturing it in runbooks, recorded walkthroughs and paired handover sessions during the notice period, as COBIT BAI08 expects, makes it an organizational asset. Retaining one engineer buys time but keeps the system dependent on a single person, who may also leave, and does not transfer knowledge to anyone else.

wrong_explanations.A: Retaining one engineer keeps a single point of failure and transfers no knowledge; the risk returns when that person leaves.
wrong_explanations.C: Old documentation rarely reflects recent changes, and six months of learning on the job with no experts leaves a live system unsupported.
wrong_explanations.D: Shutting down a system that processes samples daily causes far greater business harm than the knowledge risk it avoids.

tips: Eliminate: C ignores the gap, and D shuts down a critical system to avoid a staffing problem.
Final two: B beats A because captured knowledge outlasts any individual, while one retained engineer is still a single point of failure.

questions.question: At hour 28 of a 48-hour ERP cutover, 12,000 supplier records are found with inconsistent country codes, a case the playbook does not cover. What is the IS auditor's BEST advice?

options.A: Pause at the gate, size the fix, then proceed or revert
options.B: Proceed with the cutover and clean the supplier data after go-live
options.C: Roll back now, since the cutover plan is fundamentally flawed
options.D: Take the go/no-go decision on management's behalf to save time

questions.key_concept: Unexpected cutover issues should be assessed at a decision gate, then management proceeds or falls back based on evidence.
questions.pre_read: Notice the issue is outside the playbook. Ask which option assesses impact before committing, and who decides.
questions.correct_explanation: A sound cutover uses decision gates so that unexpected issues are assessed before commitment. Pausing to size the fix and judge whether it fits the window lets management proceed or invoke fallback on evidence. Proceeding and cleaning up later keeps the schedule, but it loads known-bad master data into production without assessing the effect on supplier transactions.

wrong_explanations.B: Proceeding loads known-bad master data into production without assessing its impact on supplier payments and orders.
wrong_explanations.C: One unforeseen data issue does not prove the whole plan is flawed. Rollback should follow an assessment, not replace it.
wrong_explanations.D: The auditor advises but must not make management's operational decisions; doing so impairs independence.

tips: Eliminate: C overreacts to one issue, and D has the auditor take a management decision.
Final two: A beats B because a risk-based decision at the gate assesses impact before committing bad data to production.

questions.question: After $14M and four months, a new CRM module has 23 of 150 targeted customers. What is the MOST appropriate basis the IS auditor should advise the board to use for its continue-or-stop decision?

options.A: Stop the module, because the $14M already spent makes recovery uneconomic
options.B: Continue, since cancelling would harm reputation and team morale
options.C: Forward costs and benefits against alternatives, excluding sunk spend
options.D: Customer survey results on why adoption is low

questions.key_concept: Investment continue-or-stop decisions compare forward costs and benefits against alternatives and exclude sunk cost.
questions.pre_read: Notice the $14M already spent. Ask whether any option uses it as a reason, and whether that reason is valid.
questions.correct_explanation: Money already spent cannot be recovered whichever way the board decides, so it must not drive the choice. The decision should compare the remaining cost and expected benefits of continuing against alternatives, such as other products or a sale of the technology. Stopping might even be right, but justifying it by the $14M already spent is the same sunk-cost error in reverse.

wrong_explanations.A: The conclusion may be right, but the stated reason is sunk cost. Past spend is irrelevant to whether future spend is worthwhile.
wrong_explanations.B: Reputation and morale matter, but they are not a decision basis on their own and invite continuing a failing investment.
wrong_explanations.D: Customer feedback is a useful input, but it says nothing about remaining costs or alternatives, so it cannot be the decision basis.

tips: Eliminate: B rests on emotion, and D treats one input, customer opinion, as the whole decision basis.
Final two: C beats A because past spend is sunk; only forward costs, benefits and alternatives should decide.
Exam cue: when a stem quotes money already spent, look for the option that explicitly excludes sunk cost.

options.B: Cancel the integration and run both firms separately

options.D: Commission an independent review and rebaseline before releasing funds

questions.correct_explanation: Spend running well ahead of delivery means the current plan cannot be trusted. An independent review that rebaselines scope, schedule and cost gives the board a reliable footing before more money is committed. Tranche funding is a good control, but tying it to milestones set by the same leadership builds gates on an unvalidated plan.

wrong_explanations.A: Approving more money on industry norms ignores the evidence that the current plan and leadership are failing.
wrong_explanations.B: Abandoning the integration discards the deal rationale and sunk progress without assessing whether recovery is feasible.
wrong_explanations.C: Gated funding helps, but gates based on an unvalidated plan from the same leadership cannot restore the board's confidence.

tips: Eliminate: A funds a failing plan as normal, and B abandons it without assessment.
Final two: D beats C because an independent rebaseline must come before gates; gates built on an unvalidated plan add little assurance.
Exam cue: when a project is far off track and confidence is lost, independent review comes before new funding.

questions.question: Facing a 22% IT budget cut, an investment committee has ranked all projects by value. Before stopping the lowest-ranked ones, what should the IS auditor recommend it confirm FIRST?

options.A: Each business unit gives up an equal share of projects
options.B: None is regulatory-mandated or a prerequisite for higher ones
options.C: Exit costs for each project proposed for stopping are known
options.D: Project managers agree with how their projects were ranked

questions.key_concept: Portfolio cuts rank investments by value and risk, then confirm no low-ranked item is mandatory or a prerequisite for higher-value work.
questions.pre_read: Notice the ranking is already done. Ask what a pure value ranking could miss before anything is stopped.
questions.correct_explanation: A value ranking can place an item low even though regulation requires it or higher-value projects depend on it. Stopping such an item would create a compliance breach or undermine the investments the cut is meant to protect, so mandates and dependencies must be confirmed first. Exit costs refine the savings estimate, but they do not show whether stopping is permissible.

wrong_explanations.A: Equal shares by unit reintroduce the uniform cut that value ranking replaced, protecting weak projects in some units.
wrong_explanations.C: Exit costs adjust the savings, but they do not reveal a mandate or dependency that makes stopping unacceptable.
wrong_explanations.D: Manager agreement is not a control; managers naturally defend their own projects regardless of value.

tips: Eliminate: A brings back a uniform cut, and D lets interested parties veto the ranking.
Final two: B beats C because a mandated or prerequisite project cannot be stopped whatever its exit cost.
Exam cue: before cutting by value, check for mandatory items and dependencies the ranking may miss.

questions.question: Management proposes insourcing 60% of outsourced application development over 24 months after vendor delays and a 28% price rise. Which input is MOST important to the IS auditor's assessment of the decision?

options.A: A multi-year business case comparing insourced and outsourced total cost
options.B: The regulator's stated concern about third-party concentration risk
options.C: Management's view that the vendor delays alone justify the change
options.D: Exit terms agreed first, then cost, capability and transition review

questions.key_concept: Insourcing decisions rest on a multi-year business case comparing the total cost of each option, made before any exit commitment.
questions.pre_read: Notice several drivers in the stem. Ask which option compares the alternatives, and whether any commits before the analysis.
questions.correct_explanation: A sourcing change is a major investment with execution risk, so the decision must rest on a multi-year business case comparing the total cost of insourcing, including capability build-up and transition, with staying outsourced. Agreeing exit terms first looks thorough because it lists every factor, but it commits the firm to leaving before the analysis shows insourcing is affordable or feasible.

wrong_explanations.B: Concentration risk is one reason to act, but it does not show whether insourcing is affordable or achievable.
wrong_explanations.C: Delays are a symptom to weigh, not a full case; a decision of this size needs cost, capability and transition analysis.
wrong_explanations.D: Every factor is listed, but exit terms come first, committing the firm to leave before analysis shows insourcing is viable.

tips: Eliminate: B and C each rest on a single driver, a regulator concern or vendor delays, rather than analysis of the decision.
Final two: A beats D because the business case must come before any exit commitment; D covers every factor in the wrong order.

questions.question: A cloud vendor hosting 70% of a hospital group's workloads announces an 18% price rise and refuses to negotiate. What should the IS auditor recommend to management as the BEST response?

options.A: Accept the increase, as any migration would cost too much
options.B: Move every workload to an alternative provider straight away
options.C: Build credible exit readiness and move portable workloads in stages
options.D: File a complaint with the regulator to force price talks

questions.key_concept: Vendor lock-in is managed through credible exit readiness and staged migration of portable workloads, improving negotiating leverage.
questions.pre_read: Notice the vendor will not negotiate. Ask which option creates leverage without taking on reckless migration risk.
questions.correct_explanation: Lock-in is reduced by making exit credible. Preparing exit plans and moving portable workloads in stages lowers concentration risk at managed cost and gives management leverage to win price or contract concessions. Moving everything at once addresses concentration, but it ignores migration cost, workloads tied to proprietary services and the operational risk of a rushed move.

wrong_explanations.A: Accepting without options rewards lock-in and leaves concentration risk unmanaged as regulators increase scrutiny.
wrong_explanations.B: An immediate full move ignores migration cost and proprietary dependencies, creating major operational risk for clinical systems.
wrong_explanations.D: Regulators do not set commercial prices. An adversarial complaint does not reduce lock-in or concentration risk.

tips: Eliminate: A accepts lock-in, and D misuses the regulator for a commercial dispute.
Final two: C beats B because staged exit readiness cuts lock-in at managed risk; a sudden full move ignores cost and dependencies.
Exam cue: for vendor lock-in, prefer credible, staged exit options over full acceptance or abrupt wholesale migration.

questions.question: Management leans toward cancelling a paused program that is $22M over budget, though three business units already use its delivered modules. Which risk should the IS auditor raise as MOST important?

options.A: Contract termination penalties payable to the vendor on exit
options.B: Reputational harm from admitting publicly that the program failed
options.C: Project team morale after the program is stopped
options.D: Disruption to live processes relying on the partial system

questions.key_concept: Cancellation decisions must weigh exit complexity, especially disruption to processes already relying on delivered components, above bounded contractual costs.
questions.pre_read: Notice that business units already use parts of the program. Ask what stopping it would do to them.
questions.correct_explanation: Cancelling is a management decision, but it must account for exit complexity. Three business units already run live processes on the delivered modules, so stopping without a transition plan could halt operations, a larger and less reversible impact than any fee. Termination penalties are a real cost to weigh, but they are bounded, contractual and quantifiable, unlike disruption to the business.

wrong_explanations.A: Penalties matter, but they are a bounded, quantifiable cost; operational disruption to dependent units carries greater and less reversible impact.
wrong_explanations.B: Reputation is a soft factor and would not justify keeping a failing program; it is not the decisive exit risk.
wrong_explanations.C: Morale affects the team, not the business processes that depend on the system, and does not change the cancellation risk.

tips: Eliminate: B weighs reputation, and C weighs team morale; neither measures business impact.
Final two: D beats A because disruption to live operations outweighs a bounded, contractual exit cost.
Exam cue: when stopping a system others rely on, weigh business continuity and exit complexity before cost.

questions.subtopic: Distributed Agile Teams Across Time Zones
questions.question: Engineering teams across six time zones report that decisions made in US hours exclude other sites and code reviews wait 18 hours. Which practice should the IS auditor consider BEST?

options.A: Require engineers at every site to work US-East business hours
options.B: Write decisions down and rotate meeting hours across sites
options.C: Consolidate engineering at the US-East headquarters site
options.D: Hold daily standups at one fixed time that suits most sites

questions.key_concept: Distributed agile teams need asynchronous, written decision-making and rotating meeting times so no site is consistently excluded.
questions.pre_read: Notice two symptoms: excluded sites and slow reviews. Ask which option fixes both without forcing everyone into one time zone.
questions.correct_explanation: Distributed teams work best when decisions do not depend on being awake at one time. Recording decisions in writing gives every site the same input, and rotating meeting hours shares the burden of awkward times. A fixed standup that suits most sites still excludes the same minority every day and does nothing for written decisions or slow reviews.

wrong_explanations.A: Forcing night work on distant sites harms retention and well-being, and the equity problem simply moves to them.
wrong_explanations.C: Closing other sites to fix coordination discards talent and capacity, a disproportionate answer to a process problem.
wrong_explanations.D: A fixed time still excludes the same sites every day and leaves spoken decisions inaccessible to those absent.

tips: Eliminate: A pushes the burden onto remote sites, and C closes sites to fix a process issue.
Final two: B beats D because written decisions and rotating hours include every site; a fixed time always excludes the same ones.
Exam cue: for distributed agile teams, prefer asynchronous, documented practices and shared burden over one dominant time zone.

questions.question: Eight product teams deploy independently to shared production, and six recent incidents came from one team's change breaking another's feature. What should the IS auditor recommend as the BEST control?

options.A: Coordinate releases by risk tier, backed by interface contracts
options.B: Require a joint sign-off from the eight teams before each release
options.C: Give each team its own separate production environment
options.D: Cut release frequency to once a month for every team

questions.key_concept: Multi-team release coordination should be risk-tiered, with interface contracts catching cross-team breaks before release.
questions.pre_read: Notice the incidents come from interactions between teams. Ask which option targets those changes without slowing all others.
questions.correct_explanation: Cross-team incidents come from changes to shared interfaces. Risk-tiered coordination, as COBIT BAI06 expects, focuses review on changes that can affect others, while interface contracts and contract tests catch breaks before release. A joint review by all teams sounds thorough, but it adds delay to every low-risk change and gives teams a reason to bypass the process.

wrong_explanations.B: Reviewing every release with all teams treats low-risk changes like high-risk ones, adding delay and encouraging workarounds.
wrong_explanations.C: Separate production environments do not reflect how shared services interact, and the integration risk returns when they connect.
wrong_explanations.D: Fewer, larger releases bundle more changes together, which raises the risk of each release rather than lowering it.

tips: Eliminate: C ignores that the services must still interact, and D makes each release larger and riskier.
Final two: A beats B because risk-based coordination targets the changes that matter, while universal review adds delay without focus.
Exam cue: for change control at scale, prefer risk-tiered controls over uniform heavy review of every change.

questions.question: In week 14 of a 20-week release, executives have added 16 features; velocity fell 28% and QA tests cover only the original scope. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Keep accepting executive requests to stay responsive to the business
options.B: Cancel the release and restart it under stricter scope rules
options.C: Put each addition through formal change control and rebaseline
options.D: Extend the test plan to cover the added features before release

questions.key_concept: Scope creep is controlled by formal change control and rebaselining, so management decides each addition on its impact.
questions.pre_read: Notice the word FIRST. Ask whether to fix the cause, uncontrolled scope, or one of its symptoms.
questions.correct_explanation: The root problem is scope entering without assessment of cost, schedule and quality impact. Routing each addition through formal change control and rebaselining the release lets management decide which features to keep, defer or fund with more time. Extending the test plan is needed, but done first it accepts every addition as given and leaves scope uncontrolled.

wrong_explanations.A: Absorbing every request is what caused the velocity drop and test gap; responsiveness without control harms release quality.
wrong_explanations.B: Cancelling 14 weeks of work overreacts. Scope can be brought back under control without discarding the release.
wrong_explanations.D: Testing the added features is necessary, but it accepts the uncontrolled scope rather than deciding what should stay.

tips: Eliminate: A feeds the problem, and B throws away most of a release to fix scope.
Final two: C beats D because controlling scope comes first; extending tests accepts every addition without assessment.
Exam cue: for scope creep, formal change control and rebaselining come before work that absorbs the extra scope.

questions.question: A new CTO proposes merging 47 microservices into about 10, citing tripled operating cost and slower delivery, although reliability has improved 25%. Which decision basis should the IS auditor consider MOST appropriate?

options.A: Aggregate operating cost and delivery speed trends since the migration
options.B: Service-by-service analysis of value, coupling, cost and ownership
options.C: The original architect's view that reliability gains justify the cost
options.D: Industry benchmarks of how many services similar firms run

questions.key_concept: Architecture reversal decisions need per-service evidence on value, coupling, cost and ownership, not aggregate trends or advocacy.
questions.pre_read: Notice the evidence points both ways. Ask which option breaks the problem down to where the costs and benefits arise.
questions.correct_explanation: Aggregate figures hide which services earn their cost. Analysing each service for the value it delivers, how tightly it is coupled to others, what it costs to run and who owns it shows where consolidation helps and where separation keeps the reliability gains. Platform-wide cost and speed trends are real evidence, but they cannot say which services to merge.

wrong_explanations.A: Platform-wide trends show a problem exists but cannot identify which services to merge, risking the reliability gains.
wrong_explanations.C: One stakeholder's view based on one metric ignores the tripled cost and slower delivery the firm is facing.
wrong_explanations.D: Benchmarks describe other firms' platforms, not which of these services earn their cost or carry the reliability gains.

tips: Eliminate: C rests on one person's view of one metric, and D relies on other firms' figures rather than this platform's.
Final two: B beats A because per-service analysis shows where to consolidate, while aggregate trends cannot.
Exam cue: for architecture reversal decisions, prefer granular evidence over aggregate metrics or advocates' positions.

questions.subtopic: Database Technology Selection. SQL vs NoSQL Trade-off
questions.question: A fleet-tracking application must ingest 1.6 million telemetry writes per second and also support relational queries. Which database selection approach should the IS auditor consider BEST?

options.A: Choose PostgreSQL alone for its ACID transactions and team familiarity
options.B: Choose an engine, then assess workload, consistency, cost and complexity
options.C: Adopt whichever product the senior database engineer prefers
options.D: Test candidate designs against both stated workloads before choosing

questions.key_concept: Technology selection should be tested against every documented workload before a choice is made, not driven by one metric or preference.
questions.pre_read: Notice the stem lists two different workloads. Ask which option proves fit to both before committing.
questions.correct_explanation: Database selection should be proven against documented requirements before committing: testing candidate designs, possibly polyglot, against both the 1.6 million writes per second and the relational queries shows which one meets them at acceptable cost and complexity. Choosing an engine first and then assessing every factor looks comprehensive, but the analysis comes after the decision, so it can only justify the choice, not inform it.

wrong_explanations.A: Team familiarity does not make a single relational engine fit 1.6 million writes per second; the ingest workload is ignored.
wrong_explanations.B: It names every factor, but in the wrong order: assessing after choosing can only justify the engine, not select it.
wrong_explanations.C: Personal preference is not a selection criterion; it skips requirements analysis entirely and risks a poor workload fit.

tips: Eliminate: A ignores the extreme write volume, and C replaces analysis with preference.
Final two: D beats B because evidence must come before the choice; B lists every factor but assesses them after committing.
Exam cue: a checklist of every factor is not the answer if it comes in the wrong order; evaluate before you decide.

questions.question: An IS auditor reviews a cloud migration plan covering strategic, stable utility and soon-to-retire applications. Which migration approach is BEST?

options.A: Refactor every application as cloud-native for one consistent architecture
options.B: Match each application's migration path to its business value
options.C: Let each app team pick rehost, replatform, refactor or retire
options.D: Rehost every application first, then refactor strategic ones after cutover

questions.key_concept: Cloud migration paths are matched to each application's business value at portfolio level, not applied uniformly or left to team preference.
questions.pre_read: Notice the portfolio mixes strategic, stable and retiring applications. Ask which approach respects those differences.
questions.correct_explanation: A mixed portfolio needs a migration path matched to each application's business value and lifespan: refactor what is strategic, replatform what is stable, rehost commodity systems and retire what is ending. Rehosting everything first sounds pragmatic, but it spends effort moving applications due for retirement and moves strategic ones twice, so the investment is not aligned to value.

wrong_explanations.A: Refactoring everything spends the most expensive treatment on stable and retiring applications that return little value from it.
wrong_explanations.C: Listing every path does not make the choice value-based; team preference replaces a portfolio decision, so costly treatments may go where value is low.
wrong_explanations.D: Rehosting everything first moves soon-to-retire applications for no benefit and makes strategic ones migrate twice.

tips: Eliminate: A applies the costliest treatment uniformly, and C leaves each path to team preference instead of business value.
Final two: B beats D because each application's path should follow its business value, not a uniform first step.
Exam cue: when a portfolio is mixed, prefer the option that differentiates by business value over any one-size-fits-all approach.

questions.question: A HIPAA-regulated firm with a flat internal network plans a zero-trust migration; the CISO wants a vendor ZTNA tool deployed everywhere at once. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Deploy the vendor ZTNA tool across every access path immediately
options.B: Micro-segment the network around the clinical systems straight away
options.C: Delay ZTNA rollout until identities, assets and flows are inventoried
options.D: Enforce MFA on clinical systems while keeping the flat network

questions.key_concept: Zero-trust starts by knowing the identities, assets and data flows to protect; enforcement tools and segmentation are designed from that baseline.
questions.pre_read: Look for the word FIRST. Ask what must be known before any zero-trust control can be designed well.
questions.correct_explanation: Zero-trust policies decide access per identity, device and resource, so the firm must know its users, assets and data flows before enforcing anything; the tool rollout should wait for that inventory, which defines the protect surfaces. Micro-segmenting clinical systems is a sound zero-trust step, but without the inventory the segments are drawn on guesswork and may break care workflows or miss sensitive data.

wrong_explanations.A: Deploying a tool everywhere before defining what to protect buys a product, not an architecture, and risks disrupting clinical access.
wrong_explanations.B: Segmentation is a valid control, but done before the inventory its boundaries rest on assumptions about assets and flows.
wrong_explanations.D: MFA strengthens logins, but on a flat network an authenticated user or compromised device can still reach everything.

tips: Eliminate: A deploys a product before any design, and D hardens logins while the flat network stays open.
Final two: C beats B because both the tool and the segments must rest on a known inventory of identities, assets and data flows.
Exam cue: when FIRST meets a big rollout, delaying enforcement until you know what you are protecting can be the right answer.

questions.subtopic: Application Zero-Day During Major Release Window
questions.question: Hours before a major release cutover, a critical exploitable flaw is disclosed in a library used by both the release and current production. Which response should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Patch the flaw in current production and the release before cutover
options.B: Proceed with cutover on schedule and patch in the next release cycle
options.C: Hold the rollout and remediate the new release build first
options.D: Suspend every release until outside researchers publish full analysis

questions.key_concept: A vulnerability shared by the release and production is scoped and fixed across every affected version, not only the build in flight.
questions.pre_read: Notice the flaw sits in both the release and current production. Ask which response closes the exposure everywhere it exists.
questions.correct_explanation: Because the vulnerable library runs in current production as well as the new release, the exposure exists today whatever happens to the rollout. The sound response scopes both versions, patches both, and then proceeds with the patched release. Holding the rollout to fix the new build feels cautious, but production stays exploitable while attention goes to the release.

wrong_explanations.B: Shipping known-vulnerable code with public exploits available accepts avoidable risk to save schedule.
wrong_explanations.C: Fixing only the new build leaves the same flaw open in production, which customers are using right now.
wrong_explanations.D: Waiting weeks for outside analysis leaves both versions exposed while a fix can be applied now.

tips: Eliminate: B knowingly ships an exploitable flaw, and D waits on outsiders while exposure continues.
Final two: A beats C because the flaw also lives in production, so fixing only the release leaves live systems exposed.
Exam cue: scope a vulnerability to every place it exists before deciding what to fix first.

questions.question: After acquiring an EU firm whose customer contracts require EU data residency, the CTO plans to move its customer data to the acquirer's US platform. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Transfer the data once standard contractual clauses are in place
options.B: Cancel the integration because cross-border data risk is unmanageable
options.C: Move the data immediately and refund any customers who object
options.D: Keep the acquired product's data in an EU-hosted region

questions.key_concept: Integration design must honor existing contractual data-residency commitments; a lawful transfer mechanism does not override what customers were promised.
questions.pre_read: Notice the residency requirement comes from customer contracts. Ask which option satisfies the contract, not just the transfer law.
questions.correct_explanation: The acquired firm promised customers that their data stays in the EU. Hosting the acquired product in an EU region lets integration proceed while keeping that commitment and GDPR transfer rules intact. Standard contractual clauses can make a transfer lawful under GDPR, but they do not cure a breach of a contractual residency promise, so moving the data would still break the agreements.

wrong_explanations.A: Contractual clauses legitimize the transfer under GDPR, yet the customer contracts still require the data to remain in the EU.
wrong_explanations.B: Cancelling ignores feasible options such as regional hosting; residency is a design constraint, not a deal-breaker.
wrong_explanations.C: Moving data first and refunding objectors knowingly breaches contracts and risks regulatory action.

tips: Eliminate: B overreacts to a solvable constraint, and C knowingly breaches customer contracts.
Final two: D beats A because a lawful transfer mechanism does not override a contractual residency commitment.

questions.question: A federal contractor must set a software supply-chain (SLSA) maturity target; the CISO wants the top level, costing about $8M over 18 months. Which recommendation by the IS auditor is BEST?

options.A: Commit to the top level now for the strongest, most defensible position
options.B: Meet the required floor first, then raise levels by risk and cost
options.C: Pick a mid level matching what peer contractors report
options.D: Attest the flagship product and leave other software lines out

questions.key_concept: Assurance targets are set by risk: meet mandatory requirements, then invest in higher maturity where risk reduction justifies the cost, with reassessment gates.
questions.pre_read: Weigh the cost figure against what is required. Ask which target is risk-based rather than maximal or minimal.
questions.correct_explanation: A maturity target should meet the mandatory attestation floor, then rise in phases where the risk reduction justifies the cost, with gates to reassess as rules evolve. Committing to the top level appears thorough, but it fixes a large spend before the firm knows which risks justify it, and it may delay meeting the current requirement while the full program is built.

wrong_explanations.A: Maximum maturity is not automatically best; an $8M commitment without risk-based justification may overshoot and delay required compliance.
wrong_explanations.C: Copying peers ignores the firm's own required floor and risk profile, so the target is neither compliance-based nor risk-based.
wrong_explanations.D: Partial scope leaves other software delivered to federal customers below the required floor and noncompliant.

tips: Eliminate: C copies peers instead of using the firm's own requirements and risk, and D leaves most software below the required floor.
Final two: B beats A because investment should follow risk and required compliance, not maximum maturity for its own sake.
Exam cue: when one option is the most thorough and another is risk-based and phased, ISACA favors risk-based.

questions.question: A supervisory authority requests privacy records; about 10% of the requested records do not exist in compliant form. What is the BEST advice from the IS auditor to management?

options.A: Submit existing records and disclose the gaps with remediation plans
options.B: Submit the compliant records and leave out the missing items
options.C: Submit existing records and dispute that the rest are required
options.D: Finish every missing record before submitting any part of the response

questions.key_concept: Regulator cooperation means timely, accurate responses: provide what exists, disclose gaps honestly, and show credible remediation plans.
questions.pre_read: Notice some records simply do not exist. Ask which response stays accurate and on time with the regulator.
questions.correct_explanation: The firm owes the authority cooperation that is both timely and accurate. Submitting existing records, disclosing the gaps openly and attaching remediation plans meets the response window and shows accountability, which regulators weigh when setting penalties. Completing every missing record first looks thorough, but it misses the deadline and produces documents created after the fact that could mislead about past compliance.

wrong_explanations.B: Silently omitting requested items misrepresents the firm's position and damages trust once the gaps surface.
wrong_explanations.C: Disputing the scope without basis undermines cooperation and does not change the fact that required records are missing.
wrong_explanations.D: Holding everything back misses the response window, and records written after the fact can misstate past compliance.

tips: Eliminate: B hides gaps from the regulator, and C disputes the request instead of cooperating.
Final two: A beats D because timely, honest disclosure with a remediation plan outranks a late response that looks complete.

questions.question: During peak season, a retailer's primary payment processor suffers an outage with no recovery estimate, and a quarterly-tested backup processor is on standby. What should management do FIRST?

options.A: Escalate the outage to the vendor under the contract's SLA terms
options.B: Integrate a new processor quickly to restore online sales today
options.C: Invoke the continuity plan and switch to the tested backup processor
options.D: Suspend online sales and notify customers until service returns

questions.key_concept: A tested continuity arrangement exists to be invoked when an outage has no recovery estimate; contractual remedies do not restore operations.
questions.pre_read: Notice the backup processor has been tested quarterly. Ask which action actually restores the business process now.
questions.correct_explanation: The continuity plan and the tested backup processor were prepared for exactly this event, and quarterly tests give evidence they work. Invoking them restores sales while the vendor recovers. Escalating under the SLA is a reasonable vendor-management step, but it only yields credits or pressure; it does not restore revenue when the vendor has no recovery estimate.

wrong_explanations.A: SLA escalation provides remedies and pressure, but it does not restore the payment process while a tested alternative sits idle.
wrong_explanations.B: An untested integration built during an incident adds failure and security risk at the worst moment.
wrong_explanations.D: Suspending sales gives up revenue unnecessarily when a tested fallback is ready to use.

tips: Eliminate: B builds an untested integration mid-incident, and D gives up revenue despite a ready fallback.
Final two: C beats A because invoking the tested plan restores operations, while an SLA claim only compensates.
Exam cue: when a tested continuity option exists and recovery time is unknown, invoke the plan.

questions.question: Two weeks before quarter close, three critical finance reports depend on rebuilt ETL jobs on a new data warehouse that are not yet validated. Which recommendation by the IS auditor is BEST?

options.A: Cut over the finance reports to the new warehouse on schedule
options.B: Delay the quarterly filing until the migration is complete
options.C: Run quarter close on the old warehouse and halt the migration
options.D: Parallel-run and reconcile the three reports to the old warehouse

questions.key_concept: Before relying on a migrated system for financial reporting, a parallel run and reconciliation provide the evidence that outputs are complete and accurate.
questions.pre_read: Notice exactly three reports are unvalidated and two weeks remain. Ask which option produces evidence for a decision.
questions.correct_explanation: Parallel running the three affected reports and reconciling them to the old warehouse produces evidence on whether the rebuilt jobs are accurate, while the old platform stays available as a fallback. Management can then decide with facts. Running close on the old warehouse and halting the migration is safe for this quarter, but it stops the whole program over three reports that may reconcile cleanly.

wrong_explanations.A: Relying on unvalidated ETL jobs for public financial reporting risks misstatement and certification exposure.
wrong_explanations.B: Public-company filing deadlines are fixed; delaying them creates regulatory breaches rather than reducing risk.
wrong_explanations.C: Halting the migration overreacts to three unvalidated reports and forgoes evidence that could resolve the issue.

tips: Eliminate: A relies on unvalidated jobs, and B treats a fixed filing deadline as optional.
Final two: D beats C because reconciliation produces evidence for the decision, while halting stops the program without it.

questions.question: Three hours after a product launch, the cloud instance quota and the database connection pool are both saturated and errors are rising. What should management do FIRST?

options.A: Request a quota increase so auto-scaling can absorb the demand
options.B: Throttle incoming traffic to protect the database while capacity grows
options.C: Halt the launch and refund every customer who has signed up
options.D: Restart the database to clear its saturated connection pool

questions.key_concept: In a capacity incident, first stabilize the constrained component; adding capacity in one layer does not fix a bottleneck in another.
questions.pre_read: Notice two components are saturated, not one. Ask which action protects the weakest point immediately.
questions.correct_explanation: Both the instance quota and the database connection pool are saturated. Throttling incoming traffic protects the database from collapse and keeps the service usable while more capacity is arranged. Requesting a quota increase sounds like the natural fix, but more application instances would open more database connections and deepen the bottleneck that is already failing.

wrong_explanations.A: More instances add database connections, so raising the quota alone can worsen the saturated pool.
wrong_explanations.C: Halting and refunding abandons the launch when the service can be stabilized by controlling load.
wrong_explanations.D: A restart drops in-flight transactions, and the pool refills at once because the incoming load is unchanged.

tips: Eliminate: C abandons a recoverable launch, and D restarts the database without reducing the load that saturated it.
Final two: B beats A because extra instances would push more load onto the already saturated database.
Exam cue: when several layers are saturated, stabilize the shared constraint before adding capacity elsewhere.

questions.question: An IS auditor finds a CRM-to-billing sync job has failed silently for four months, leaving 720 customer records inconsistent. Which recommendation is BEST?

options.A: Fix the root cause, correct records, add reconciliation monitoring
options.B: Reconcile the 720 affected records in a one-time cleanup effort
options.C: Halt customer-facing operations while the records are corrected
options.D: Add a manual billing check for each new customer record

questions.key_concept: Data-integrity failures need root-cause correction and detective monitoring; cleaning up affected records alone leaves the cause and the detection gap.
questions.pre_read: Notice the failure was silent for four months. Ask which option stops it recurring and makes it visible next time.
questions.correct_explanation: The real weaknesses are a faulty interface and the absence of any control that would have detected it. Fixing the root cause, correcting the affected records and adding reconciliation monitoring stops new errors, repairs existing ones and surfaces any future failure quickly. A one-time cleanup corrects today's records, but the job keeps producing errors and nobody would notice them for months again.

wrong_explanations.B: A cleanup corrects existing records, but the faulty job keeps creating new mismatches and nothing detects them.
wrong_explanations.C: Stopping operations for a few hundred records is disproportionate when targeted correction is possible.
wrong_explanations.D: Checking new records adds manual effort but leaves the 720 existing errors and the faulty job in place.

tips: Eliminate: C is a disproportionate shutdown, and D adds manual checks on new records while the cause and old errors remain.
Final two: A beats B because it repairs the records and also fixes the cause and adds monitoring, while cleanup only treats symptoms.
Exam cue: when a failure went undetected, the best answer fixes the cause and adds a detective control.

questions.question: An organization is setting up a project management office (PMO). Which function should be its PRIMARY role?

options.A: Executing project work directly in place of project managers
options.B: Deciding which proposed projects receive funding and priority
options.C: Setting standards and methods and supporting project managers
options.D: Auditing closed projects to assign blame for any overruns

questions.key_concept: A PMO enables project delivery through standards, methods, support and consolidated reporting; funding and priority decisions sit with portfolio governance.
questions.pre_read: Separate the PMO from the bodies that fund projects. Ask which role supports delivery rather than governs investment.
questions.correct_explanation: A PMO's primary role is to make project delivery consistent: it sets standards and methods, supports project managers and consolidates reporting for leadership. Deciding which projects receive funding sounds like a PMO task, but that investment decision belongs to the steering committee or portfolio governance body; the PMO informs it with data rather than owning it.

wrong_explanations.A: A PMO supports project managers; it does not replace them or carry out the delivery work itself.
wrong_explanations.B: Funding and prioritization are decided by the steering committee or portfolio board, which the PMO supports with information.
wrong_explanations.D: Post-project reviews aim at lessons learned, not blame, and they are not the PMO's primary purpose.

tips: Eliminate: A replaces project managers, and D turns reviews into blame.
Final two: C beats B because funding decisions belong to the steering committee; the PMO enables delivery.

questions.question: A project steering committee is choosing a development method. In which situation is prototyping MOST appropriate?

options.A: Requirements are stable and fully documented at project start
options.B: Users want to see screens early, though requirements are signed off
options.C: Throwaway prototype code would cost more than the final system
options.D: Users cannot state requirements until they use a working model

questions.key_concept: Prototyping suits uncertain or evolving requirements that users refine by interacting with a working model; stable requirements favor a planned sequential approach.
questions.pre_read: Focus on how certain the requirements are. Ask where interacting with a model adds the most value.
questions.correct_explanation: Prototyping earns its cost when requirements are unclear and users can only define them by trying a working model; each iteration turns feedback into firmer requirements. Users wanting to see screens early sounds like a prototyping case, but the requirements are already agreed, so a prototype adds review effort without resolving any real uncertainty.

wrong_explanations.A: Stable, documented requirements fit a planned sequential method; prototyping adds iterations without reducing uncertainty.
wrong_explanations.B: With requirements signed off, early screens are a presentation preference rather than a reason to change method.
wrong_explanations.C: When prototype costs outweigh the system's value, prototyping is uneconomic and should be avoided.

tips: Eliminate: A has stable requirements, and C makes the prototype uneconomic.
Final two: D beats B because prototyping resolves requirements uncertainty, and B has none left to resolve.
Exam cue: match the method to requirements certainty: uncertain favors prototyping or iteration, stable favors sequential.

questions.question: A development team adopts a code generator to produce application modules. Which control should the IS auditor consider MOST important?

options.A: Apply peer review, testing and version control to generated code
options.B: Validate and formally approve the generator tool before first use
options.C: Ban generators and require developers to hand-write the code
options.D: Accept the vendor's assurance that generated output is secure

questions.key_concept: Generated code is source code: it goes through the same review, testing and configuration management as hand-written code before reaching production.
questions.pre_read: Think about what actually reaches production. Ask which control examines that output every time.
questions.correct_explanation: What reaches production is the generated code, and its quality depends on inputs, templates and configuration that change over time. Treating it as source under peer review, testing and version control checks every output. Validating the generator before first use is a sensible step, but a one-time approval of the tool cannot catch defects in later outputs.

wrong_explanations.B: A one-time tool approval does not examine each module produced later, so defective or insecure output can still pass.
wrong_explanations.C: Banning generators gives up productivity without addressing risk; the issue is control over output, not the tool.
wrong_explanations.D: Vendor assurance covers the tool generally, not the specific code produced for this application.

tips: Eliminate: C discards a usable tool, and D relies on a vendor claim about generic output.
Final two: A beats B because ongoing control of each output outranks a one-time approval of the tool.

questions.question: A bank's regulated payments platform has passed development testing, and the CIO wants to skip formal accreditation to protect the timeline. Which recommendation by the IS auditor is BEST?

options.A: Complete an independent control certification, then release on its results
options.B: Have an authorized official accept residual risk before deployment
options.C: Treat passing development tests as sufficient evidence for release
options.D: Accredit the platform after go-live using production feedback

questions.key_concept: Accreditation is a management decision: an authorized official accepts residual risk on the basis of certification evidence before the system goes live.
questions.pre_read: Ask who owns the decision to accept risk on a regulated system, and when it must happen.
questions.correct_explanation: Accreditation is the formal management decision in which an authorized official reviews certification evidence and accepts the residual risk before the system operates, keeping accountability with management. Independent certification sounds rigorous, but it evaluates whether controls work; it is evidence for the decision, not the decision, so releasing on its results still skips the accountable risk acceptance.

wrong_explanations.A: Certification tests controls and informs the decision, but without an authorized official accepting residual risk, no one is accountable for releasing.
wrong_explanations.C: Development testing shows functions work but does not document control evidence or formal risk acceptance.
wrong_explanations.D: Accreditation is a pre-deployment gate; doing it after go-live leaves customers exposed to unaccepted risk.

tips: Eliminate: C confuses testing with accreditation, and D moves the gate to after go-live.
Final two: B beats A because certification supplies evidence, while accreditation is management's accountable acceptance of residual risk.

questions.question: An IS auditor reviews a traditional waterfall project plan. Which phase sequence is MOST appropriate?

options.A: Design, requirements, build, test, deploy, maintain
options.B: Requirements, design, test, build, deploy, maintain
options.C: Requirements, design, build, deploy, test, maintain
options.D: Requirements, design, build, test, deploy, maintain

questions.key_concept: Waterfall runs requirements, design, build, test, deploy, maintain, with sign-off at each gate before the next phase starts.
questions.pre_read: Check two anchors: requirements before design, and testing before deployment.
questions.correct_explanation: Waterfall is a gated sequence: requirements are baselined, a design is produced from them, the system is built, then tested against the requirements before it is deployed and maintained. Deploying before testing keeps the other phases in order, which makes it tempting, but it releases unverified code into production and removes the gate that testing is meant to provide.

wrong_explanations.A: Design cannot come first; it answers requirements that have not yet been defined.
wrong_explanations.B: Testing cannot precede build because there is nothing yet built to test.
wrong_explanations.C: Deploying before testing releases unverified code and defeats the pre-deployment gate.

tips: Eliminate: A designs before requirements exist, and B tests before anything is built.
Final two: D beats C because testing must gate deployment, not follow it.
Exam cue: anchor on requirements before design and test before deploy; any option breaking either is wrong.

questions.subtopic: CI/CD. Continuous Delivery vs Continuous Deployment
questions.question: An IS auditor reviews a pipeline described as continuous deployment. Which feature MOST distinguishes it from continuous delivery?

options.A: Passing builds reach production with no manual approval step
options.B: Developers merge code into the main branch several times daily
options.C: The pipeline serves web applications rather than mobile ones
options.D: It adds integration tests to the unit tests that delivery runs

questions.key_concept: Continuous delivery keeps every build releasable with a manual release decision; continuous deployment removes that gate and releases automatically.
questions.pre_read: Both practices share frequent integration and automated testing. Ask what happens at the production release step.
questions.correct_explanation: Both practices keep code integrated and tested automatically; the difference is the release step. Continuous delivery stops for a manual approval before production, while continuous deployment sends every passing build straight to production, so automated controls must replace that human gate. Frequent merging to the main branch is real, but it describes continuous integration, which both practices share.

wrong_explanations.B: Frequent merging is continuous integration, a foundation of both practices, so it does not distinguish them.
wrong_explanations.C: Neither practice is tied to an application type; both apply to web, mobile and other systems.
wrong_explanations.D: Both practices run automated test suites at several levels; test scope is not the defining difference.

tips: Eliminate: C ties the practice to a platform, and D invents a difference in test scope.
Final two: A beats B because frequent merging is shared continuous integration; only the release gate differs.
Exam cue: delivery means a human approves the release; deployment means the pipeline releases automatically.

questions.subtopic: User Acceptance Testing. Purpose and Timing
questions.question: A project manager is scheduling user acceptance testing (UAT) for a new billing system. When is UAT MOST appropriately performed?

options.A: During construction, as each module is completed
options.B: In parallel with system testing to shorten the schedule
options.C: After go-live, using live transactions in production
options.D: After system testing passes, in a production-like environment

questions.key_concept: UAT follows successful system testing and precedes cutover, with business users testing in a production-like environment.
questions.pre_read: Place UAT in the test sequence. Ask what must be stable before business users can accept the system.
questions.correct_explanation: UAT is the final acceptance gate: business users confirm the system meets their requirements once system testing has removed technical defects, using a production-like environment and data so results reflect real use, and before cutover. Running UAT alongside system testing saves time, but users then test a moving build, find defects the test team should catch, and may accept a version that later changes.

wrong_explanations.A: Module-level checks during construction are unit testing by developers; business acceptance needs the integrated system.
wrong_explanations.B: Overlapping with system testing means users accept an unstable build that may still change after their sign-off.
wrong_explanations.C: Acceptance after go-live is too late; the business would be using a system it never accepted.

tips: Eliminate: A is unit-level work during build, and C accepts the system only after it is live.
Final two: D beats B because acceptance should rest on a stable, system-tested build, not one still changing.

questions.question: A change manager is aligning the change process with ITIL 4 change enablement. Which set of change types is MOST consistent with ITIL 4?

options.A: Major, minor and patch
options.B: Standard, normal and emergency
options.C: Approved, pending and rejected
options.D: Routine, planned and unplanned

questions.key_concept: ITIL 4 change types are standard (pre-authorized, low risk), normal (assessed and authorized) and emergency (expedited authorization).
questions.pre_read: Separate change types from release numbering and approval status. Ask which set reflects how a change is authorized.
questions.correct_explanation: ITIL 4 groups changes by how they are authorized: standard changes are low-risk and pre-authorized, normal changes go through assessment and authorization, and emergency changes get expedited authorization. Routine, planned and unplanned sounds like an equivalent scheme, but it describes scheduling rather than authorization path and is not ITIL terminology, so it would not map to defined approval routes.

wrong_explanations.A: Major, minor and patch describe release or version numbering, not change authorization types.
wrong_explanations.C: Approved, pending and rejected are statuses a change request moves through, not types of change.
wrong_explanations.D: These terms describe scheduling, not the authorization route, and are not ITIL 4 change types.

tips: Eliminate: A is version numbering, and C lists request statuses.
Final two: B beats D because ITIL 4 types reflect how a change is authorized, not how it is scheduled.
Exam cue: standard means pre-authorized, normal means assessed, emergency means expedited authorization.

questions.question: A firm has a source code escrow agreement for critical software from a small vendor. Which control BEST assures the deposit would be usable if released?

options.A: The vendor's own annual written confirmation that deposits are current
options.B: Contract terms defining release triggers such as vendor insolvency
options.C: Annual agent verification that the deposit builds the live version
options.D: Storing the deposit with the vendor's own legal counsel

questions.key_concept: Escrow assurance requires independent, periodic verification that the deposit is complete, current and builds the production version.
questions.pre_read: Ask what happens if the vendor fails tomorrow and the deposit is outdated.
questions.correct_explanation: Escrow only protects the licensee if the deposited material can actually rebuild the software in use. Periodic verification by the escrow agent, compiling the deposit and comparing it with the live version, provides that evidence. Clear release triggers are essential, but they only determine when the code is handed over, not whether what is handed over will work.

wrong_explanations.A: A vendor's own confirmation is self-assertion; it does not show the deposit is complete or will build.
wrong_explanations.B: Triggers decide when code is released, but a stale or incomplete deposit is useless when it arrives.
wrong_explanations.D: The vendor's counsel is not independent, so the licensee cannot rely on access when the vendor fails.

tips: Eliminate: A relies on vendor self-assertion, and D leaves the deposit with a party that is not independent.
Final two: C beats B because triggers govern when code is released, while verification proves it will work.
Exam cue: for escrow assurance, an independent periodic test build beats any vendor assertion, however often it is made.
